stories.headline: In Keralam, ‘affordable’ private health care is easier said than done
stories.deck: Keralam government’s efforts to draft a new Bill in this regard brings the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, back into focus; the private health sector is still holding out against the Act, which aims to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework
stories.bodyText:
The Keralam government’s announcement that it will make private health care more “affordable” through consultations with the private health sector, and that a Bill in this regard was in the offing, should be seen against the State’s seven-year legal battle before the Kerala High Court upheld the Kerala Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulations) Act 2018, throwing out all objections raised by private hospitals.
The KCE Act was the first ever attempt made in the State to bring the entire health sector, public and private, under a regulatory framework.
But the Act was systematically opposed and its implementation stalled at every turn by the private health sector in the State.
It was in November last year that the Kerala High Court threw out all objections raised by the Kerala Private Hospitals’ Association (KPHA) and the Indian Medical Association (IMA) and upheld the validity of the Act.
Contentious area
Unlike the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010 (Central Act 23 of 2010), which attempted to cap the treatment/procedure/diagnostic rates charged by the private health sector by fixing a price range, the KCE Act had not touched this contentious area at all.
The KCE Act just insisted on mandatory registration of all clinical establishments under all systems of medicines (including hospitals, clinics and laboratories) and that every establishment maintain certain minimum standards based on the category in which they fall. It also said that hospitals display their rates for various procedures openly so that there is transparency.
However, the private health sector argued that it violated rights under Article 14 and Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.
Appeal in SC
Even after the High Court specifically held that KCE Act’s Section 16 (mandatory registration of clinical establishments), Section 39 (display of fee rates and package rates for services) and Section 47 (obligations concerning life-saving treatment/emergency care and safe transfer of patients) were constitutionally valid and gave directives to the government to implement the Act without delay, KPHA went in appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court has not stayed the KCE Act, but granted members of the petitioning associations interim protection against coercive action by the government.
Yet to register
Kerala Clinical Establishments Council, which is responsible for the implementation of the Act, maintains that the registration process is continuing and that even now, many clinical establishments are yet to register themselves under the council.
Small hospitals with up to 15 beds have been given some concessions by the council, trimming down the checklist for assessment to just basic and essential points, so that at least the basic registration brings these establishments too within the regulatory framework.
The government’s efforts to draft a new Bill to bring in a regulatory framework that “protects patients’ interests while taking into account the operating costs and practical difficulties of private hospitals” is well-intentioned, but the fact remains that the private health sector is still holding out against the KCE Act at the Supreme Court.
Questions are also being raised whether a new legislation is in order or if the costing regulations can be incorporated into the KCE Act itself.
‘Entirely welcome’
Meanwhile, public health activists like B. Ekbal have stated that any attempt by the government to regulate the treatment expenditure in the private sector and save people from catastrophic health expenditure is entirely welcome.
Dr. Ekbal said that though private hospitals are an essential component of the health system, health care cannot be left entirely to market logic. It is the government’s responsibility to regulate the sector adequately so that patients are not exploited.
In a statement here, Dr. Ekbal said that the Standard Treatment Guidelines (STGs) should be insisted on and that the government initiate a scientific cost evaluation of various medical and diagnostic procedures and treatments so that a rational and transparent rate list suited to the State can be evolved.

stories.headline: Bengal bypolls: Humayun Kabir detained in Murshidabad after casting vote
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AJUP) chief and MLA 
Humayun Kabir
 was briefly detained by Rejinagar Police and taken away from his party office in Murshidabad on Tuesday, after he cast his vote in the Rejinagar Assembly constituency by-election.
Voting began early Tuesday for by-elections to five Assembly seats across West Bengal, Tamil Nadu and Puducherry, along with a Lok Sabha seat in Assam.
In West Bengal, polling is being held in the Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly constituencies. The Nandigram seat fell vacant after Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari won from two constituencies in the state Assembly elections earlier this year and chose to retain the other seat.
The Rejinagar seat fell vacant after Kabir, who had won from both Rejinagar and Nowda, resigned from one of the constituencies.
The Rejinagar contest includes BJP nominee Sakharav Sarkar, former Murshidabad district president; Mamata Banerjee-led TMC candidate Rabiul Alam Chowdhury; rival TMC candidate Safiuzzaman Sheikh; Congress nominee Mohammad Abdullahil Kafi; and CPI(M)'s Syed Asad Ali.

The administration has put in place multi-layered security arrangements to maintain law and order and ensure peaceful polling, officials said.

stories.headline: Pretty in pink, but Malarikkal’s lilies worry ecologists
stories.deck: A two-year study for the Kerala State Biodiversity Board finds the water lily, which appeared in Malarikkal after the 2018 floods, has shown unprecedented and uncontrolled growth; ecologists flag its impact on local aquatic plants, water flow and sunlight penetration, besides concerns over methane emissions from decaying plant biomass; the seasonal bloom has transformed Malarikkal into a tourism…
stories.bodyText:
The profuse blooming of pink water lilies in Malarikkal may have brought joy to hundreds of visitors and local tour operators, but not to biodiversity experts.
The three-month-long floral economy, which begins in July and ensures a flurry of activity and generates revenue, is having an adverse impact on the local ecology, ecologists fear.
A two-year-long study carried out for the Kerala State Biodiversity Board (KSBB) has revealed that the lily, an aquatic plant, has shown unprecedented and uncontrolled growth, adversely affecting the ecology.
Rameshkumar K.B., senior principal scientist at the Jawaharlal Nehru Tropical Botanic Garden and Research Institute, who has been carrying out the study, said the water lily appeared in the region after the 2018 floods and showed prolific growth.
“The plant did not exist previously in the region, and research is ongoing to confirm whether the species could have escaped from nurseries or is a variant of an existing species. Studies are being carried out at the genetic and molecular levels to ascertain the species,” he said.
N. Anil Kumar, Chairperson of the Board, said the uncontrolled growth of the plant was alarming and needed to be prevented so that it did not spread to other water bodies.
“The ecological impact on the species in the water body needs to be studied further. We need strict control measures to prevent such species from deeply infiltrating into our ecology, and eventually decimating the local flora,” said Mr. Anil Kumar.
According to the study, the water lily has led to an increase in the rodent population and the disappearance of local varieties of water lilies and other aquatic plants. The release of greenhouse gases such as methane from decaying plant material is a major concern, said Mr. Rameshkumar.
“With millions of water lilies blooming, they are attracting pollinators significantly, and this may affect the pollination pattern of land crops in the future. It has affected the natural rate of water flow. The sedimentation of sludge as well as decayed plant biomass has led to the water bodies getting polluted. Traditional water transportation has also been affected,” said Mr. Rameshkumar.
Another concern is the vast coverage of the water surface by the large leaves, which affects the penetration of sunlight into the water body. He noted that this could be negatively impacting the habitats of algae and other micro- and macro-organisms inside the water body.
As the species emerges as a threat to the ecology and threatens to spread to more regions, locals are, however, rejoicing at the unexpected revenue they have received.
The water lily blooms every year from July, after paddy cultivation in the region. Ever since the pink bloom appeared, the tourism economy has exploded.
The water lily blooms across two main paddy parcels in Malarikkal in Kuttanad. One of the land parcels, J Block, is spread across 1,800 acres and is held by 600 farmers, while Thiruvaikkari Padam, which spans about 850 acres, is held by 300 farmers.
“Majority of the owners have country boats, which they use during the season to take tourists across the water body. Around 250 country boats are in use during this time,” said Shajimon Vattappallil, secretary, Malarikkal Tourism Society.
He added that he regularly gets calls from nearby farmers asking how they can replicate this.
“I tell them they cannot imitate this, but they can try collecting some of the water lily roots and try planting them,” said Mr. Vattappallil.
Residents of the area say the bloom has benefited people in the region, including women who make bouquets, as well as farmers who rely on the tourist footfall for additional income.
K. Anilkumar, coordinator of the Meenachil-Meenanthayar-Kodoor river rejoining project, said a revenue of about ₹5 crore was generated last year.
“It brings additional income for the farmers and the locals,” said Mr. Anilkumar.

briefs.headline: 19,000 West Bengal voters to miss bypolls as appeals remain pending in tribunals
briefs.deck: Out of the 19 Appellate Tribunals set up by the Election Commission in March, only 16 remain functional, as three retired judges — Justice T.S. Sivagnanam, Justice Ranjit Bag and Justice Indrajit Chatterjee — have quit, citing various functional issues. Their positions remain vacant.
briefs.bodyText:
Nearly 19,000 voters in West Bengal’s Nandigram and Rejinagar Assembly constituencies, where byelections are being held on Tuesday (October 6, 2026), are among the 38.31 lakh voters in West Bengal who remain disenfranchised due to the crawling pace of work at the Appellate Tribunals where their cases are pending. The Calcutta High Court had in July observed that at the current rate, it would take 21 years for the tribunals to clear the cases.
In Rejinagar, the total number of appeals submitted was 12,452, out of which four have been included so far, and in Nandigram, the total number of appeals submitted was 6,443, with 89 included so far. While in both places, no one has been excluded so far, the tribunals have, till now, cleared only 1.26 lakh of the total 38.31 lakh appeals, which is approximately 3% of the total cases.
Out of the 19 Appellate Tribunals set up by the Election Commission (ECI) in March, only 16 remain functional, as three retired judges — Justice T.S. Sivagnanam, Justice Ranjit Bag and Justice Indrajit Chatterjee — have quit, citing various functional issues. Their positions remain vacant.
The ECI’s proposal to increase the number of tribunals from 19 to 42 has also not moved forward. The Supreme Court was scheduled to hear the matter on Monday (October 5), but it was not listed.
The poll body’s special “door-to-door” drive to re-enrol any voter left behind during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process through Form 6, announced last week, will also not be applicable to them.
The Appellate Tribunals came out of the Supreme Court’s supervision of the SIR. Judicial officers, drawn from a list the Calcutta High Court sent at the Supreme Court’s direction, were adjudicating the roughly 60 lakh “doubtful and pending” cases. On March 10, the top court had directed that a separate appellate body be set up so that people could challenge those officers’ decisions.
Of the roughly 60 lakh “doubtful” cases, the 700 judicial officers cleared and restored approximately 32.77 lakh (32,77,360) voters onto the electoral rolls. The remaining 27.23 lakh were rejected, of whom 22 lakh appealed to the tribunals.
The ECI constituted the Appellate Tribunals for West Bengal on March 21. The tribunals began functioning around April 13, and on April 16, the Supreme Court ordered that voters whose appeals succeed be added through a supplementary list. The verdict came only days before Assembly elections began on April 23, and reportedly only 136 names had been cleared by then.
Parallelly, 16,10,311 bulk appeals were instituted at the Appellate Tribunals challenging the decision to include voters restored by the judicial officers, bringing the total number of cases pending in the tribunals to a little more than 38 lakh.

briefs.headline: Most of rural agricultural workers landed in non-productive, informal urban jobs in 25 years: study
briefs.deck: Study based on RBI’s KLEMS data says agricultural labourers moved to non-productive sectors such as restaurants, construction and transport
briefs.bodyText:
A study on the productivity gap in farm and non-farm sectors, published in the Journal of Development Economics and authored jointly by economists Rajveer Jat and Bharat Ramaswami, has found that labourers from the agriculture sector, who shifted to cities, were pushed towards non-productive sectors such as transport and restaurants, making no substantial changes either in the economy or in their lives. It said that between 63% and 75% of non-farm workers are in informal employment-dominated industries that are not more productive than agriculture.
The authors suggest policy reforms, including expansion of education and healthcare facilities, to help those who migrated from the agricultural and rural economic sectors to find vocations in productive sectors around cities. The study is based on the data sourced from the Reserve Bank of India’s KLEMS (Capital, Labour, Energy, Materials and Services) data since 1999 till 2024.
Small productivity gap
The study pointed out that the productivity gap between agriculture and the informal non-farm sector is small or negligible once differences in labour share, human capital, and hours worked are accounted for. “In fact, 63-75% of non-farm workers are in industries whose productivity is statistically indistinguishable from that of agriculture. By contrast, the formal non-farm sector is substantially more productive: even after adjustments, its value-added per worker is two to three times higher than that of agriculture,” the study found and added that the large aggregate agricultural productivity gap (APG) is therefore driven primarily by the small but economically dominant formal segment of the non-farm economy.
The paper added that the real “structural dualism” in the Indian economy is between the high-productivity formal sector and the low-productivity informal sector (including agriculture), not simply between “farm” and “non-farm”.
The labour mobility between agriculture and the informal sector, the study noted, appeared relatively unconstrained as workers could move freely between them. “Much of the uncorrected productivity gap between them arises because of greater hours of employment in the informal sector. Therefore, even if the corrected productivity gap is low, the seasonality of agricultural activity is a reason to migrate,” it said.
Living standards
Talking to The Hindu, Mr. Jat said typically non-agriculture sector is more productive and labour from agriculture are pulled out and put into non-agriculture so that if they work in high productive environment, the overall living standards of a country rises. “That’s how development stories have been in many of the countries,” he said but added that a country should empower its labour force to move to more productive sectors such as Information Technology or finance sectors.
“We should move people more into those sectors instead of the restaurant sector or construction or any other non-agriculture activities which are not productive,” Mr. Jat said adding that the barriers for the labour force to entry into the formal sectors are lack of formal education, which is a college degree, and lack of English education, which is a doorway to more productive sectors such as IT and financial services.

briefs.headline: DVAC launches probe into the alleged sand mining scam during the DMK government
briefs.deck: A detailed inquiry was ordered on the basis of a complaint filed by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) which alleged serious irregularities in the mining of river sand across Tamil Nadu
briefs.bodyText:
The ED said in a report that the survey revealed mining beyond permissible limits. The value of the illegally mined sand was quantified at ₹4,730 crore, which the investigators alleged was the proceeds of crime
The Directorate of Vigilance and Anti-Corruption (DVAC) has launched an investigation into the alleged ₹4,730-crore sand mining scam which had taken place during the previous DMK government.
A detailed inquiry was ordered on the basis of a complaint filed by the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) which alleged serious irregularities in the mining of river sand across Tamil Nadu, official sources said on Monday (October 5, 2026).
Notice sent
The DVAC has sent notice to the contractors, officials, and others involved in the scam as part of the detailed inquiry which is usually conducted for establishing prima facie offence before a case is registered, the sources said.
The central agency had written to the Tamil Nadu Director-General of Police on June 13, 2024, giving evidence of the illegal sand mining and requesting registration of a First Information Report. A reminder was sent to the DGP on July 18 that year, but no action was taken.
The ED had registered a case of illegal sand mining under the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002. Investigators collected evidence by deploying advanced scientific techniques with the assistance of experts associated with a company incubated at the Indian Institute of Technology, Kanpur.
The quantum of illegal sand excavated was assessed across all 28 river-sand mining sites with the help of advanced techniques.
The ED said in a report that the survey revealed mining beyond permissible limits. The value of the illegally mined sand was quantified at ₹4,730 crore, which the investigators alleged was the proceeds of crime.
ED relies on GPS data
ED officials also relied on the GPS data provided by the company which had sold the excavators used by the contractors. The technical data — precise GPS co-ordinates, Geo Scanning, and Geo Fencing — provided by the company revealed the details of operational hours and excavation timings of the machines at precise locations.
“The ED compared the data with the GPS coordinates of the permitted quarries and the number of machines permissible under the State government rules. The findings conclusively established that the subject excavators were deployed and operated beyond the demarcated boundaries,” the agency said.

briefs.headline: In Japan, women’s sumo battles tradition and a male-dominated system for survival
briefs.deck: More than 100 women gathered at the Kyoto City Budo Centre to practice sumo wrestling. Despite historic resistance, female participation in sumo is increasing, with over 600 women involved in various clubs. The Japan Sumo Association does not recognise women's sumo, leaving many to rely on private clubs for training. Coaches and athletes express hope for future Olympic inclusion as they work to…
briefs.bodyText:
KYOTO: It’s a rainy Sunday morning but that hasn’t stopped more than 100 women and girls from making their way to the Kyoto City Budo Centre, Japan’s oldest martial arts performance hall. Built in 1899, the original structure is mostly out of bounds for visitors. But a recently built adjoining hall is buzzing with activity.
The women are dressed in wrestling singlets, wearing the traditional mawashi, the thick belt associated with sumo, over it. At the centre of the hall is a ring that looks like a dohyo, the raised platform on which sumo is contested. It looks like one. But it isn’t.
Women are traditionally barred from stepping into a sumo dohyo, a practice rooted in religious beliefs that have long associated menstruation with impurity. Yet, inside this hall, women are doing precisely what tradition has told them they cannot: sumo wrestling.
More than 600 women in over 70 clubs practise the traditional form of wrestling in Japan, despite the resistance it has faced. In the wrestling venue at the Asian Games, when a senior official of the Japan Wrestling Association was asked about women’s sumo, he laughed before dismissing it: “It’s no sport for women.”
But it wasn’t always this way. Historical research suggests women participated in sumo as far back as the fifth century. The sport also had periods of popularity between 1603 and 1868 and in the early 20th century, before women’s sumo was banned in 1926 on moral and traditional grounds.
It returned in organised form in 1997. Yet, amateur women’s sumo continues to fight for survival. The Japan Sumo Association does not recognise it, leaving private clubs, schools and universities to keep it alive.
At universities and a few clubs, women train alongside their male counterparts. Even the arrival of Japan’s first female prime minister has not changed the equation. Sanae Takaichi, who became prime minister last year, had said, “I respect tradition. I will not step on the dohyo.”
There are, however, women like Airi Hisano, considered the strongest woman sumo wrestler of the country, trying to change things. The 27-yearold Tokyo native began with karate and judo before finding her calling in sumo at Nihon University.
She was fortunate to find support at home. “My family wants me to do my best,” she said.
It wasn’t easy. “Of course people made fun of me because, in rigid gender spaces, acceptance wasn’t easy. But that didn’t bother me. Also, it wasn’t an Olympic sport,” said Airi, who works in the administrative section of Tachihi Holdings.
A heavyweight competitor, Airi balances training with her day job, where she also doubles as a security guard. She holds a third-degree black belt in judo and a first-degree black belt in karate. “We still have a long way to go,” she said.
Not far from where Airi was preparing for her bout, Katsumasa Kawase was putting three girls from Team Shiga through their warm-up. “Being a sumo wrestler myself, I didn’t want my daughters to be denied the opportunity when they wanted to try it,” Kawase said, helping his daughters Momoka and Yuzuki warm up.
The physical demands are no different from those faced by their male counterparts. The typical diet includes chicken or pork, vegetables, rice and candied sweet potatoes. But muscle is not the biggest hurdle. Awareness is.
Morita, who handles public relations for Yoko Sumo Club, an all-women’s team based in Tokyo, said the club was formed in 2024 and has remained exclusively female. “A major challenge is that many people are still unfamiliar with women’s sumo,” she said.
What keeps the wrestlers going? “They continue believing that the sport will eventually be included in the Olympics,” Morita said.
Women coaches are still few. One of them is Mao Ueda of Hirakata Sumo Club. A former judoka and jiu-jitsu practitioner, she took up coaching after seeing an opportunity to combine her experience in martial arts with the nuances of sumo.
“It’s a long road,” she said. The biggest challenge, she believes, comes after university. “With no recognition, money or future, most girls drop out after university. We need a structure to change that,” Ueda said.
However, Momoka, 9, knows little about any of that. Two years into the sport, she knows only that she wants to become an Olympian.

briefs.headline: UN chief calls for Gaza ceasefire ahead of October 7 anniversary
briefs.deck: Antonio Guterres also said Palestinians in Gaza have faced a “massive loss of life, displacement and destruction,” without specifying their death toll
briefs.bodyText:
United Nations Secretary General Antonio Guterres on Monday (October 5, 2026) called for a permanent ceasefire in Gaza ahead of the third anniversary of the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel.
“It is time for the ceasefire to become permanent. It is time to allow humanitarian assistance at scale. And it is time to respect international law,” Mr. Guterres said in a statement, calling for a “political path to lasting peace across the whole region.”
“Let this anniversary mark not only another year of mourning, but also a renewed determination to build a different future: one in which Israelis and Palestinians can live side by side in peace and security, with their rights, dignity, and aspirations fulfilled,” Mr. Guterres said.
The UN chief acknowledged Israel’s casualties in the statement, calling the Hamas attack “abhorrent” for “killing more than 1,200 Israelis and foreign nationals” and the hostage-taking of another 251 people.
Mr. Guterres also said Palestinians in Gaza have faced a “massive loss of life, displacement and destruction,” without specifying their death toll.
“Their suffering, too, demands an end, now,” Mr. Guterres said.
Israel’s years-long military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 74,200 people according to the Palestinian Health Ministry, which is under Hamas’ authority and whose figures are deemed reliable by the UN.
Mr. Guterres acknowledged that a brief ceasefire, announced by U.S. President Donald Trump in October 2025, “brought some relief. But it has yet to deliver security, adequate humanitarian assistance or a credible path to recovery and peace.”
Israel, which still controls most of Gaza, refuses to withdraw its soldiers until Hamas’ disarmament has been verified.
Hamas, for its part, has advocated for gradual disarmament rather than immediate and unilateral surrender of its arsenal.
Since the 2023 attacks, Israel has waged military attacks on several fronts, notably invading southern Lebanon to confront Hezbollah, the Islamist movement backed by Tehran, and launching war against Iran in late February alongside the United States.

briefs.headline: Nazis and the bomb: nuclear archaeology finds Werner Heisenberg mistook how close he was
briefs.deck: Scientists have found that the Nobel laureate may have grossly overestimated how close his team was to having a working nuclear reactor, much less a nuclear weapon
briefs.bodyText:
Hans Bethe. Felix Bloch. Niels Bohr. Albert Einstein. Enrico Fermi. James Franck. Otto Frisch. Samuel Goudsmit. Lilli Hornig. Rolf Landshoff. Maria Goeppert Mayer. Rudolf Peierls. George Placzek. Eugene Rabinowitch. Joseph Rotblat. Leo Szilard. Edward Teller. Stanislaw Ulam. John von Neumann. Victor Weisskopf. Eugene Wigner. These are just some of the scientists who had emigrated from Europe, many of whom later made critical contributions to the Manhattan Project — the American effort to build the world’s first nuclear weapon.
Many of these scientists had seen firsthand the horrors Nazi Germany was perpetrating in Europe; many were Jews who were escaping persecution themselves. They showed their contempt for Adolf Hitler and his armies by bringing a sense of urgency to their research on the bomb, and were often motivated by what they believed the stake was: the fate of the world itself.
The Manhattan Project tested its first atom bomb on July 16, 1945, and delivered two to the U.S. military in July-August. Part of their sense of urgency was rooted in doubts about whether Nazi Germany was also building a bomb, including an effort led by physicist and Nobel laureate Werner Heisenberg. Their anxieties were not unfounded: in April 1945, only weeks before Germany surrendered to Allied forces, Heisenberg’s team had assembled a nuclear reactor in a cellar beneath a church in Haigerloch, in the country’s south.
The setup, called the B8 pile, had 664 cubes of uranium suspended on chains in around 1,400 litres of heavy water. A 40-cm-thick shell of graphite surrounded the core, and was itself surrounded by a layer of aluminium and a 60-cm-thick layer of (ordinary) water. Heisenberg’s team had taken six years to build B8 but had little to show for it. When a few neutrons were shot into the reactor, the uranium multiplied them into more — but no chain reaction followed.
Far from critical
After the war ended, Heisenberg said the team had come very close; he wrote in a 1947 article in Nature that Haigerloch didn’t have enough resources and that just a little more quantity of uranium would have done the trick.
According to a new study in PNAS Nexus, by researchers from the U.S., Heisenberg & co. were actually way off the mark.
Only around 14 of the 1,100 or so uranium cubes made for Heisenberg’s efforts still survive. Using a pycnometer, the team found the density of one cube to be 18.535 g/cm3, lower than the 19.01 g/cm3 of solid uranium, indicating the cube was porous. Another cube contained 0.724% of uranium-235 (by mass), meaning it was natural rather than enriched uranium.
In March 1944, a German physicist named Karl Wirtz had reported that Nazi Germany’s stocks of heavy water had accidentally been diluted to 98.85% purity. A post-war sample from Haigerloch in 1947 found only 96.8% purity. The team also started from the records of aluminium giant Norsk Hydro to estimate that Nazi Germany had a maximum supply of 1,836 kg of pure heavy water during the war.
When the team worked upwards from here, including the design of the B8 pile, they concluded it had a neutron multiplication factor of 0.942. A reactor needs to have a factor of 1 to be critical, and a difference of 0.058 is actually large. The team found that the uranium cubes in B8 were arranged too close together, preventing the heavy water from efficiently slowing the neutrons. The researchers estimated that increasing the heavy water’s purity to 100% would improve the factor to only 0.95.
They also simulated over 1,200 combinations of uranium and heavy water and found that the B8 pile would have required at least 2,994 kg of uranium and 3,411 litres of heavy water to become critical. B8 however, contained 1,538 kg of uranium and 1,549 kg of heavy water when it was dismantled. More importantly, the team also estimated all German facilities at the time combined possessed only 2,572 kg of uranium and 1,890 kg of 96.8%-pure heavy water — a significant shortfall and which could support a factor of 0.959 at best.
Industrial capacity
The first U.S. reactor, called Chicago Pile-1, first became critical on December 2, 1942, using natural uranium as fuel and graphite, rather than heavy water, as the moderator. So some nuclear historians have opined that Heisenberg et al. had simply picked the wrong moderator.
A 2025 study in The European Physical Journal H demurred, however: while the U.S. was able to source petroleum coke extremely low in boron and turn it into reactor-grade graphite, the graphite made from metallurgical coke in Germany was high in boron, which absorbs neutrons. The B8 pile used the graphite from the predecessor B7 pile, and the new study also found that it contained 3.4 weight-parts per million (wppm) of equivalent boron contamination. The Siemens graphite from earlier contained around 6.6 wppm. On the other hand, the Manhattan Project used graphite with around 1.4 wppm of boron. In simulations, it didn’t matter how far apart the uranium cubes in the B7 pile or in any previous piles could have been: the contamination made criticality impossible.
The significant difference between the Nazi German and the Manhattan Project programmes, then, seems to have been industrial capacity. The Americans developed and built multiple technologies to enrich uranium, set up reactors and chemical separation units, and a weapons laboratory, which together created 1.3 lakh jobs and invested $2.2 billion at the peak. Nazi Germany had nothing of similar scale.
Understandable concerns
According to a 2015 study in Angewandte Chemie, some uranium from the Nazi nuclear programme had not experienced a significant neutron flux and had probably come from Joachimsthal in today’s Czechia, indicating (in a limited sense) the absence of an industrial uranium enrichment programme.
Many questions about the Nazi nuclear programme still remain open, often rooted in different interpretations of common data. Some important ones are centered on whether German scientists deliberately delayed the bomb project. Some technical questions are open, too. For example, the purity of the heavy water at Haigerloch itself is unknown and the graphite’s boron content is based on archival rather than direct, firsthand information.
The overall picture today is neither that German physicists were incompetent nor that they were tantalisingly close to building a bomb. Their base of materials fell short of what a nuclear programme required and their supply chains were not good enough. Ultimately, given the information available at the time, and more so given Germany was also home to many of the world’s best nuclear physicists, the Manhattan Project scientists’ concerns were understandable.

briefs.headline: Accenture CEO rejects concerns that AI is a threat to the company’s business model
briefs.deck: Accenture's CEO Julie Sweet shared insights on significant advancements in artificial intelligence impacting the company. Over 400 clients have started advanced AI projects in the past fiscal year. The company recorded fourth-quarter revenue growth fueled by AI-driven efficiencies and client transformation integration. Additionally, productivity enhancements have allowed for executing larger…
briefs.bodyText:
Artificial intelligence is proving to be a dual engine for Accenture, driving customer demand while boosting internal productivity, CEO Julie Sweet announced during the company’s fourth-quarter earnings call. The Dublin-headquartered professional services giant reported that approximately 100 additional clients kicked off their first advanced AI projects in the fourth quarter. That pushed the total number of enterprise clients initiating advanced AI engagements with the firm past 400 for the fiscal year.
Sweet once again rejected concerns that automation might undermine the traditional IT services model, describing AI efficiencies as a structural advantage rather than a business threat. “Our strategy is to lean into these efficiencies precisely because they create value for our clients while continuing to invest and rotate our capabilities to capture the larger growth opportunities AI creates,” Sweet said. “That is why we continue to view AI as a tailwind for Accenture.”
The technology's momentum was reflected in fourth-quarter financial results. Accenture posted quarterly revenue of $18.7 billion, up 6 percent year-over-year, alongside new bookings of $22.2 billion, a 4 percent increase. 
For the full fiscal year, total revenue reached $74.2 billion, up by $4.5 billion. Investors responded swiftly to the earnings release, sending the company’s stock up more than 17 percent to trade around $214 on Thursday.
‘AI driving efficiency at Accenture, leading to bottomline growth’
“AI is now embedded across all of our work,” Sweet said on the call, noting that the company is integrating the technology early into client transformations spanning consulting, managed services, and ecosystem collaborations. “When you think about seven percent growth in every market, in consulting type of work, managed service and positive growth in every industry, the big growth drivers for the quarter were our large-scale reinventions, the ecosystem, and data and AI.”
Beyond driving client engagements, AI-driven automation is directly lifting Accenture’s bottom line. Sweet highlighted that productivity enhancements boosted revenue per employee in 2026, allowing the firm to execute larger, more complex projects without expanding headcount at the same rate as revenue growth. While Accenture plans to continue hiring across all global markets in 2027—including at entry levels, the overall pace of recruitment will moderate as automated systems absorb routine operational loads.
This is not the first time that Accenture CEO has spoken about the company leaning heavily into AI. In March this year, while announcing the company's second quarter of Fiscal Year 2026, Sweet said, "We play a critical role in the AI ecosystem,” she said. “Our role is helping clients understand what to deploy and when, how to integrate it into their systems, reimagine their processes, modernize their data and digital core, and help build the capabilities and talent needed to scale across the enterprise."
“We see AI as a tailwind because it’s helping us win more today and take market share,” she said. “It is creating new opportunities for growth over time.”

stories.headline: Karnataka OKs auto approval of period leave for govt staff
stories.deck: The Karnataka government has made significant improvements to the menstrual leave application process for women in government roles. Now, approvals will be automatic via the Kartyavya app, streamlining what was once a cumbersome and delayed endeavor. This new approach eliminates scrutiny from authorities and guarantees that approvals are not held up, making menstrual leave a clear and accessible…
stories.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Women govt employees across Karnataka will no longer need to justify their need for menstrual leave with their sanctioning authority, as the state govt Monday ordered automatic approval of all such leave applications through the Kartyavya app.
In a move aimed at ensuring menstrual leave remains an entitlement rather than a matter of discretion, the latest directive from the Praja Seva department has made the leave-sanctioning process virtually automatic, eliminating the need for human intervention. Officials have been instructed to ensure that employees apply for menstrual leave only through the Kartyavya app.
App-authorised leave can’t be reversed
The Kartyavya app is an AI-powered mobile attendance registration platform. Once a menstrual leave application is authorised through the app, no sanctioning authority can withhold, question or reverse the decision.
The decision follows recent reports that women employees were facing hurdles in availing the leave, with applications allegedly being held up and some sanctioning officers even questioning the need for such leave.
The state govt has now made it clear that such discretion cannot be exercised once the prescribed conditions are met. The circular issued by Praja Seva department said state govt had already extended a day’s menstrual leave every month to women govt employees. The benefit was specifically introduced to do away with the need for a medical certificate.
“An application that fulfils the prescribed conditions should be sanctioned promptly, and the sanctioning authority has no discretion to reject it,” the circular further clarified.

stories.headline: Karnataka plans nine industrial townships in Bangalore Metropolitan Region
stories.bodyText:
The Karnataka government plans to set up nine integrated industrial townships in the Bengaluru Metropolitan Region (BMR), with 13,500 acres identified for the projects, as the State prepares a 10-15 year development plan for the region.
Of the land required, about 7,900 acres has already been acquired and acquisition of another 5,600 acres is under way, Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar said on Monday after a review meeting on the economic development of the BMR.
The plan, prepared by the State government with the ISEG Foundation, identifies technology, high-tech manufacturing, healthcare and education, infrastructure and sustainability, and planned urbanisation and housing as the five areas expected to drive the region’s growth.
The government is also looking to develop an AI City on the lines of Singapore’s Punggol and an AI university. Mr. Shivakumar directed officials to identify suitable land for both.
The meeting also discussed expanding the metro network by 312 km by 2037 and increasing suburban rail connectivity. A 210-km ring road connecting 10 additional hubs and linking Phase 2 of the Peripheral Ring Road with NICE Road were among the proposals. A 270-km Regional Rapid Transit System connecting Bengaluru with Tumakuru, Mysuru and KGF was also discussed. The government is considering extending the proposed Mumbai-Bengaluru high-speed rail corridor up to Mysuru.
The BMR is projected to require 3,600 million litres of water a day by 2037. The government plans to prepare a plan for the region’s drinking water and industrial water requirements, with the Chief Minister directing officials to focus on treated-water reuse and lake rejuvenation.
The government has also proposed constructing 6-6.5 lakh houses, including 40,000-50,000 houses for industrial workers. The plan also proposes mapping the entire road network in Bengaluru Urban district and bringing areas not covered by the Bengaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board.

stories.headline: 10-year plan: Nine townships, 312km Metro, 210km ring road to take pressure off Bengaluru
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The nucleus of growth will soon shift from core city areas to suburbs. Govt has plans to establish nine integrated industrial townships, expand mass transit, build new housing and region-wide water and sewage infrastructure across Bengaluru Metropolitan Region in the next decade.
Chairing a meeting of the advisory committee on BMR’s economic development Monday, chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
 said the renewed infrastructure push comes against the backdrop of the state’s larger goal of taking its economy to a $1-trillion mark by 2047.
For integrated industrial townships, govt has already acquired 7,900 acres, while acquisition of another 5,600 acres is under way. “I’ve instructed officials to identify suitable land for setting up an AI university and AI city, which we want to develop along the lines of Singapore’s Punggol,” Shivakumar said.
Punggol is said to be Singapore’s first modern smart and sustainable eco-town. It was a fishing and farming village earlier.
Amid concerns over frequent traffic snarls, CM said govt is considering 312km additional Metro lines, 210km ring road, 270-km RRTS network and expanded suburban rail connectivity as part of a larger development plan for BMR in the next 10 years.
“The 210-km ring road will link 10 additional hubs and connect Phase II of Peripheral Ring Road (PRR) with NICE Road. 
The RRTS will connect Bengaluru with neighbouring districts such as Tumakuru, Mysuru and KGF,” CM said.
Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda said the entire Bengaluru Urban district will eventually come under the ambit of Bengaluru Water Supply and Sewerage Board (BWSSB). The move is expected to facilitate the expansion of water distribution and sewage networks beyond the existing serviced areas.

stories.headline: Chandapura sees hours-long traffic jam as weekend return rush peaks
stories.deck: Many people who had travelled towards Hosur on Friday night for the long weekend began returning to Bengaluru on Monday morning as offices and schools reopened. This added to the usual morning rush on the already congested stretch.
stories.bodyText:
A heavy Monday morning rush brought traffic on the Chandapura stretch to a standstill for several hours, with vehicles returning to Bengaluru after the long weekend adding to the congestion. Office-goers said they were stuck from around 7 a.m., while some school students reached school nearly three hours late.
Many people who had travelled towards Hosur on Friday night for the long weekend began returning to Bengaluru on Monday morning as offices and schools reopened. This added to the usual morning rush on the already congested stretch.
Rajesh K., a resident of the area, said he left home at 7 a.m. expecting traffic but was still delayed by nearly two hours. “Even two-wheelers had no space to move,” he said.
Residents told The Hindu that the stretch has been seeing heavy traffic for some time due to ongoing road work and poor road conditions, which have slowed down traffic. The situation was worse on Monday morning, they said.
School students were also caught in the traffic, with some having examinations on Monday. Residents said school buses and vans were stuck for hours and could not take other routes. The traffic was further affected by the narrow stretch near the railway track, where police and civic workers were clearing stagnant rainwater. The work took up part of the already narrow road and added to the traffic.
Traffic police were deployed to regulate the movement of vehicles and clear the bottleneck. The police said it took more than two hours for traffic movement to return to normal.
A traffic police officer said the existing two-lane stretch near the railway track needs to be widened to four lanes to prevent traffic from building up. “Widening the road from two lanes to four lanes at the railway track would significantly ease traffic movement and prevent such bottlenecks,” the officer said.

briefs.headline: Central draft rules: Druggists in Bengaluru oppose preserving CCTV visuals for 90 days
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: With Union health ministry proposing significant amendments to Drugs Rules, 1945, city-based chemists have flagged concerns related to regulations on CCTV surveillance.
As a regulatory measure, govt recommended mandatory CCTV surveillance at medical stores. While that could enhance transparency and accountability, pharmacists in Bengaluru feel preservation of CCTV recordings for three months should be dropped or substantially reconsidered from the final rules.
The ministry had last month published the draft gazette notification with an aim to address concerns relating to unauthorised access to and sale of Schedule H, H1 and X drugs.
The proposal was initially discussed by Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) and subsequently circulated among members of Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB), which gave the green signal.
In an appeal to central govt, Bangalore District Chemists’ and Druggists’ Association (BDCDA) argued that CCTV systems should be used for accountability and not to criminalise retail pharmacies.
BDCDA president B Thirunavukkarasu said CCTV should be a tool for accountability and not become a mechanism for creating constant fear among retail pharmacists. 
“A retailer should be able to conduct legitimate day-to-day business without living under the fear that every interaction, every transaction and every operational moment could subsequently become the subject of scrutiny, complaints or harassment,” he added.
Pharmacists fear compulsory retention and production of recordings could potentially increase opportunities for interference, harassment and corrupt practices unless strict safeguards, access controls and accountability mechanisms are prescribed.
“I have been running a medical shop in Bengaluru for more than 40 years; we have always embraced technology and even without the mandate, my shop has CCTV. There is no necessity to have a backup of 90 days,” said Laxman Raja, who runs a pharmacy in Malleswaram.

briefs.headline: PGCET students protest outside KEA office in Bengaluru, demand second round of counselling
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Students staged a demonstration outside the Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA) office Monday demanding a second round of counselling for PGCET (Postgraduate Common Entrance Test), which holds the key to MBA, MCA and MTech seats.
The results of the first round of counselling were announced in the last week of Sept. A total of 23,164 seats were allotted: 11,462 seats for MBA, 8,093 for MCA, and 3,609 for MTech. As many as 9,574 seats in MCA, 2,195 in MBA, and 1,821 in MTech remain unallocated.
However, KEA hasn’t released the choice-entry results or announced the schedule for a second round. According to students, the delay is making it difficult for them to plan their admissions, arrange finances and make other preparations for the academic year.
All India Students’ Association said: “A single counselling round cannot equitably distribute professional postgraduate seats. Leaving admissions halted after round 1 or denying standard subsequent rounds violates natural justice and established precedent. Candidates have an established right to hold an allotted seat while seeking higher preference upgrades. Bypassing the standard post allotment choice-entry system (choice 1 to freeze, choice 2 to hold and upgrade, choice 3 to surrender and retry, choice 4 to exit) forces candidates to either accept an unsatisfactory seat or drop out entirely.
”
The association also highlighted that while national PG entrance exams declare results in 25-35 days, KEA has taken three months. KEA, however, said the onus for the delayed result was on 
Visvesvaraya Technological University
, which had to send the UG marks.
The seat matrix for PGCET was also delayed. With this, counselling also did not start early. Meanwhile, private universities have already completed admissions to their seats and have started classes.
KEA officials said Karnataka govt has approached the 
Supreme Court
 seeking an extension of deadline for admissions. “If SC gives an extension, we’ll conduct another round of counselling,” said an official. “The seat matrix for PGCET was also delayed from the higher education department,” he added.
A student said: “The whole system is skewed. They are robbing poor students of opportunities. Those who can afford it take seats in private universities. The others are left in the lurch as govt takes its time for everything.”
Scuffle on premises
A scuffle broke out on the KEA premises as students demanded to meet the executive director. However, officials said the two students who had come and submitted a memorandum were from a student political organisation. “They had come in at a time when confidential answer scripts of a recruitment exam were being brought to the KEA office. They were therefore not allowed into the building. Their memoranda have been taken,” said a KEA official.

briefs.headline: Youth steals copper from same shop over 20 times in Karnataka, gets caught
briefs.bodyText:
Chikkaballapur: A 25-year-old man was arrested in Chikkaballapur for allegedly stealing copper scrap from the same shop more than 20 times over the past year, with the stolen material estimated to be worth nearly Rs 9 lakh. The accused, Saleem, was caught during a late-night theft and has been remanded in judicial custody.
The accused, reportedly a drug addict, committed theft of scrap copper from one of the scrap shops in Chikkaballapur and sold it to different purchasers in various places in Bengaluru Rural and other parts, said Musheer Ahmed, owner of Syndicate Scrap shop.
Musheer, who has been in the scrap business for the past few years, began noticing copper scrap and other materials going missing from his shop frequently in recent months. Following road-widening works in Gauribidanuru and Sidlaghatta, several old buildings were demolished, and Musheer had purchased discarded electrical items and wiring material. After sorting the copper components, he stored them separately at his shop.
He installed CCTV cameras and discovered that a youth was entering the shop after midnight to steal the copper. Musheer and a few employees attempted to catch the thief by keeping vigil at the shop overnight. 
However, the accused managed to evade them on a couple of occasions, taking advantage of nights when it was raining heavily.
Musheer subsequently approached the Chikkaballapur police for help. Acting on their directions, he and a couple of police officers kept watch at the shop one night and caught Saleem red-handed while he was allegedly stealing the copper.
Police later learnt that two other youths were involved in the thefts and would remain outside the shop, keeping watch on the movements of Musheer and his staff. Efforts are on to trace and arrest the two.
According to Musheer, Saleem allegedly stole copper scrap worth nearly Rs 9 lakh in more than 20 visits to the shop over the past year.

briefs.headline: Vinegar, chilli powder, shattered knees: Bengaluru techie’s chilling AI queries before triple murder
briefs.deck: In a shocking incident in Seegehalli, Bengaluru, techie J Kenneth allegedly murdered his partner's family. He had used artificial intelligence to research various methods of attack prior to the crime. Shwetha, Kenneth's partner, had borrowed substantial loans to support him, causing family tension. Following a confrontation with her parents about the loans, Kenneth reportedly carried out the…
briefs.bodyText:
BENGALURU: Investigation into the June triple murder at Seegehalli, KR Pura, has culminated in a chilling revelation: before allegedly turning violent against his live-in partner’s family, 25-year-old techie J Kenneth allegedly used artificial intelligence (AI) to explore possible ways of attacking people.
His queries included methods involving a kitchen knife, delivering fatal blows, blinding victims with vinegar and chilli powder, and incapacitating them by attacking their knees.
Cops stumbled upon these details in the search history on Kenneth’s laptop, which had a disturbing pattern of AI-related searches. The questions, cops said, appeared to explore different attack scenarios and how people could be overpowered.
Among the questions that surfaced in the search history were: how to fatally attack people with a kitchen knife; how to blind people using vinegar, chilli powder and chilli paste; how to shatter the knees of three people; and how to knock down three thieves who had entered a house in an isolated location.
Kenneth also asked AI about the history of some of the deadliest weapons used to kill people. In another line of questioning, he sought advice on dealing with repeated calls from banks over a friend’s loan and asked how bankruptcy could be declared.
For police, the sequence of questions has assumed significance because they came before Kenneth allegedly attacked his live-in partner Shwetha’s parents and sister inside their apartment on June 22.
“He never asked AI what the punishment for murder would be or whether it was right to kill people who were questioning his financial inability,” a senior police officer said. “He regularly chatted with AI and treated it like a friend. He may have been academically good, but his practical knowledge and social behaviour appeared extremely poor.”
Police, however, are yet to establish what answers AI provided to Kenneth. The questions were noted from the dropdown window that appeared on Google while the forensic science laboratory examined the laptop and other material.
The investigation has also thrown up a striking physical detail from the crime scene: a bottle containing vinegar mixed with chilli powder. “We’ve sent it to the FSL for examination,” DCP (Whitefield division) Saidulu Adavat said.
Money, rows  and fatal assault
The motive of the crime, according to the 2,085-page chargesheet filed before the city court, was rooted in money and mounting pressure on Shwetha.
Shwetha, also a techie, had raised loans totalling Rs 52 lakh for Kenneth within a year. This included a Rs 30-lakh business loan, personal loans of Rs 8 lakh and Rs 6 lakh from two banks, and another Rs 8 lakh borrowed from friends, relatives, classmates and colleagues.
With repayments not being made, officials of the bank that sanctioned the business loan sent a notice to Shwetha’s parents’ home.
That was when the parents — Somasundar, 55, and Muthulakshmi, 50 — learnt that their daughter had borrowed a substantial amount of money, allegedly to support Kenneth. The discovery triggered a confrontation between Shwetha and her parents.
Somasundar subsequently confronted Kenneth, questioning him about what he had done with the money and why the family was receiving notices over unpaid loans.
Days later, on the night of June 22, the row ended in bloodshed inside their apartment at Sai Green Apartment complex in Seegehalli. Somasundar, Muthulakshmi, and their 20-year-old daughter Supriya were allegedly attacked.
Somasundar, who suffered multiple injuries, managed to flee the apartment and reached the staircase. He told security personnel and others that Kenneth was attacking his wife and daughter inside.
He was rushed to a private hospital but later died. Muthulakshmi and Supriya, found with multiple stab injuries, succumbed as well.
In her statement recorded in court, Shwetha narrated how Kenneth allegedly attacked her parents and sister while she watched, the chargesheet says.

briefs.headline: 62 lakh properties in Bengaluru, but only 18 lakh owners pay tax, says minister Krishna Byre Gowda
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Bengaluru development minister Krishna Byre Gowda says the city’s biggest property tax challenge is not a lack of revenue potential but low compliance, with only around 18 lakh properties currently paying taxes despite estimates suggesting there are between 47 lakh and 62 lakh properties.
In a recent interaction with
TOI, Gowda said the city’s corporations are facing financial stress because a large number of property owners remain outside the tax net or are under-reporting their liabilities while continuing to avail civic services.
According to the minister, different datasets, including socio-economic surveys and electricity connection records, suggest that Bengaluru has far more properties than those reflected in tax records. While surveys estimate the number of properties at over 47 lakh, Bescom records show nearly 62 lakh electricity connections across the city.
Despite this, only around 18 lakh properties are paying property taxes, he said.
The minister also flagged under-reporting among existing taxpayers. Citing a sample study of 23,000 properties, Gowda said: “Our estimate is that these 23,000 properties may be underpaying around Rs 700 crore in taxes.”
Gowda argued that widening tax base is crucial not only for improving civic finances but also for ensuring fairness among residents. He said compliant taxpayers often end up carrying a disproportionate burden while neighbouring properties enjoy the same civic amenities without contributing adequately.
“A law-abiding citizen does not need recognition from govt. What they need is for everyone else to comply as well. It is unfair when one person pays taxes while another who enjoys the same services pays nothing,” he said.
Noting that property tax guidance values haven’t been revised since 2016, Gowda said govt is currently focused on improving compliance rather than increasing rates. “By simply bringing non-tax-paying and underpaying properties into the tax net, corporations can improve their finances and deliver better services without having to depend on higher taxes from those who are already paying,” he said.
As part of this effort, the state is working on integrating various civic databases, mapping properties and assigning unique identifiers to identify properties that have escaped assessment.
Officials are also examining incentives and disincentives to improve compliance. According to the minister, only about 23 lakh properties have obtained khata records, highlighting the challenge of tracking a large number of properties that remain outside formal civic records despite availing services such as water and electricity connections. “The first task is identification. We need to map properties, identify who is paying, who is underpaying and who is not paying at all,” he said.
The minister added that improving compliance would strengthen the finances of the city’s corporations and support investments in roads, water supply, sanitation and other civic infrastructure.

briefs.headline: Uncertainty over second round of PGCET counselling makes aspirants anxious
briefs.deck: The Karnataka Examinations Authority has extended the fee payment deadline three times for candidates allotted seats in the first round, with payment now mandated by October 7, 2026
briefs.bodyText:
Uncertainty looms over whether the second round of counselling for PGCET courses, including MBA, MCA, ME, MTech, and MArch, will be conducted or not, leaving seat aspirants anxious.
The Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA) has extended the fee payment deadline three times for candidates allotted seats in the first round, with payment now mandated by October 7, 2026. Additionally, candidates have been given until October 8 to download their seat confirmation slips and secure admission at their respective colleges after paying the fees.
However, seat aspirants have expressed frustration with KEA for failing to provide any information regarding the second round of counselling. Demanding that the process for “choice entry” for the second round be opened, aspirants have submitted an online petition bearing the signatures of 6,508 candidates.
When aspirants visited the KEA office on Monday (October 5) seeking clarification, a heated verbal altercation ensued between them and officials. The candidates staged a protest, expressing outrage after KEA staff attempted to forcibly remove them from the premises.
“Thousands of candidates are in a state of confusion due to the lack of information regarding the second round. Despite repeatedly requesting that the ‘choice entry’ for the second round be opened, there has been no response. When we visited the KEA office to seek information, the staff assaulted us and tried to drive us out,” the candidates alleged.
Source of confusion
The PGCET counselling has been delayed this year due to several factors, including a delay by the Department of Technical Education in submitting the seat matrix.
Meanwhile, the All India Council for Technical Education (AICTE), having released the academic schedule for postgraduate (PG) courses, mandated that classes should commence on October 15. As the admission processes were not yet complete, several States approached the Supreme Court seeking an extension of the enrolment deadline for PG courses. However, the Supreme Court directed that the AICTE schedule be adhered to.
Therefore, the results of the first round of seat allotment were announced on September 25, 2026, by KEA. A total of 23,164 seats were allotted in the first round. Consequently, 9,574 MCA seats, 2,195 MBA seats, and 1,821 MTech seats remain unallocated. The KEA said that the schedule for the subsequent admission process would be announced after September 29.
However, instead of announcing the schedule for the second round of admissions, the authorities have extended the deadlines for fee payment and college admission regarding the first-round seats three times.
Online petition
Candidates, left in a state of deep confusion by this move, have started an online petition demanding the commencement of the ‘choice entry’ process for the second round of admissions. Students are facing considerable difficulties in planning their admissions, arranging finances, and making the necessary preparations for the upcoming academic year. stories.headline: Oil prices hover near $100 as Middle East supply holds up, Gulf risks persist
stories.deck: Oil prices are currently around $100 a barrel as stable Middle Eastern exports ease supply concerns. However, ongoing regional conflicts, including Houthi attacks, raise risks of disruptions. Officials indicate that rebuilding global oil stockpiles could take years due to significant withdrawals. Industry executives predict that demand recovery may not occur until 2028 or 2029. Prices may…
stories.bodyText:
Oil prices remained close to $100 a barrel on Tuesday, with steady Middle Eastern oil exports helping to ease supply concerns. However, continued attacks in the region kept traders alert to the risk of disruptions to Gulf supplies.
Brent crude was trading at $100.6 a barrel, up 24 cents or 0.24%, while WTI stood at $89.60, gaining 17 cents or 0.19%.
The benchmarks have eased from around $103 a barrel after shipping data showed Middle Eastern crude exports had exceeded pre-war levels on four days in the final week of September. Oil shipments held up despite attacks on vessels travelling through the Strait of Hormuz.
The supply picture also improved after G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves. The group also pledged not to restrict energy exports following pressure from US President Donald Trump.
But the stronger oil flows have not removed concerns about future supplies, with fresh attacks adding to uncertainty over Gulf shipments.
Houthi attacks keep Gulf supply risks alive
Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis said on Monday that they had attacked several sites in Saudi Arabia, including King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh and Abha airport. 
Saudi Arabia had not immediately confirmed the attacks.
The attacks came as US-Iran talks remained at a stalemate, while the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthi forces continued to raise concerns about possible disruptions to supplies from Saudi Arabia, the region's largest oil exporter.
"Without a clear diplomatic breakthrough or a further material improvement in export efficiency, the floor under prices looks reasonably firm," Waterer said.
Supply squeeze could last
The concerns around supply could persist well beyond the immediate crisis. Oil industry executives at a conference in London on Monday said shipping bottlenecks, deep cuts in refinery output and inventory withdrawals that could take years to replace could keep global oil prices high beyond this year.
The Strait of Hormuz has been a major source of disruption since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran at the end of February, when Iran effectively closed the waterway and choked exports through the crucial shipping route.
The disruption has been compounded by attacks on oil and gas infrastructure, which have hampered production and affected exports of crude oil and refined fuels.
"I think it is going to be bedlam for the bulk of the end of the year and maybe 2027," Petronas CEO Tengku Muhammad Taufik said.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser said it could take up to two years to rebuild global oil stockpiles that have been drawn down as an emergency measure.
Speaking at the Energy Intelligence Forum in London in his first conference address since the start of the Iran war, Nasser said the scale of the stockpile withdrawals would make replenishment a long process.
"Until Hormuz fully re-opens and confidence returns, the crude reality is that pressure at both ends of the barrel will intensify. Even then, replenishing inventories while meeting demand could take up to two years," he said.
Nasser said 3 billion barrels had been lost since the start of the conflict, while 1 billion barrels had been withdrawn from global inventories. The reference to both ends of the barrel covers unrefined crude as well as refined products such as diesel and jet fuel.
Demand recovery may take longer
The supply disruption could also affect the timeline for a recovery in global oil demand.
ConocoPhillips Executive Chair Ryan Lance said demand could take until 2028 or 2029 to recover from this year's decline, although he expects it to grow after that.
Lance said the floor for US benchmark WTI crude would rise to around $70 a barrel, with a mid-cycle price of $65 to $70 a barrel.
US oil production could exceed 14 million to 14.5 million barrels per day if prices remain strong, he said, although he did not specify what he meant by strong prices.
Brent futures had traded just above $100 a barrel on Monday, while WTI was close to $90, keeping both benchmarks elevated as traders balanced stronger Middle Eastern exports against the continuing risk of supply disruptions.

stories.headline: SEBI to partly reverse derivative settlement rules after pushback, sources say
stories.deck: SEBI told it had received 20,000 suggestions to tweak the rules in response to a consultation paper issued last month
stories.bodyText:
India’s markets regulator is likely to stop using closing auctions to calculate derivatives settlement prices for at least a year, two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said, in a partial reversal of new mechanisms it has introduced for setting the closing prices of key stocks and derivative contracts.
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in August introduced a new mechanism called the closing auction session, or CAS, for stocks that have futures and options contracts linked to them.
Under this system, a short auction at the end of the trading day helps determine the closing price of a stock. The new process, similar to that used in global markets including the U.S. and Hong Kong, has led to sharp swings in derivatives prices on expiry days, prompting the regulator to review it.
In a post on X over the weekend, SEBI said it had received 20,000 suggestions to tweak the rules in response to a consultation paper issued last month.
Sources said that instead, the volume-weighted average price of the last 30 minutes of trading will be used to determine the derivative pricing.
For underlying stocks in the less liquid cash market, a closing auction will still be used to determine the end-of-day price, said the sources, who declined to be identified as they are not authorised to speak to the media.
SEBI is expected to implement the changes by the end of this month.
A SEBI spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
The new approach would align India more closely with US and European markets, where derivatives settlement is often determined using dedicated pricing mechanisms, including volume-weighted average prices over set trading periods, rather than a single closing auction.
Roadmap to full implementation
The regulator had also proposed in its review plans in September to stop publishing the indicative value of an index and publish only the indicative prices of individual stocks during the 10-minute CAS window, arguing that the index value was still being determined.
The majority of feedback comments it received said that sophisticated trading desks could reconstruct those values independently and that removing them would reduce transparency without addressing manipulation concerns, the sources said.
“The regulator agrees but will push for greater awareness among investors that the underlying index price is only determined at the end of the 10-minute window,” said the second source.
The feedback also favoured keeping the existing timetable broadly intact, with regular trading continuing until 3:30 p.m. and derivatives trading until 3:45 p.m., as this would aid price discovery and better align derivatives trading with the cash market closing process.

stories.headline: MSMEs seek curbs on steel, metal price surge; urge Centre to cut import duties
stories.deck: The industry body said timely intervention was essential to contain input-cost pressures and protect the competitiveness and viability of the region’s MSME sector.
stories.bodyText:
Coimbatore’s Micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), already reeling under higher prices of diesel, furnace oil and LPG, are facing mounting pressure from a sharp rise in the cost of key raw materials such as steel, pig iron, copper and aluminium.
The Joint Council of Associations of Coimbatore, in a memorandum submitted to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, said the “acute and unprecedented” increase in raw material prices was placing severe stress on MSMEs.
While Wholesale Price Index (WPI) data indicate fluctuations and even a decline in steel prices, actual market conditions remain “adverse”, the council said. Steel prices have risen by around ₹8,000-₹10,000 a tonne between August and September this year, it added.
The council urged the government to constitute a Price Monitoring Committee for steel to track availability and prices and prevent hoarding, cartelisation and abnormal price increases.
It also sought withdrawal of applicable import and safeguard duties on steel for six months and deferment of the Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) requirements and Quality Control Orders for imported steel until March 2027.
To address shortages of non-ferrous metals, the council called for measures to encourage imports of copper and aluminium scrap. It also urged the Union government to take measures on a “war footing” to secure copper and aluminium scrap from the European Union through engagement with the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
The council further sought the fixing of a Maximum Retail Price (MRP) for essential raw materials to prevent arbitrary price increases.
It also urged the Ministry of Steel to explore setting up a SAIL depot in Coimbatore to ensure easy and timely availability of quality steel to MSMEs in Coimbatore and neighbouring industrial regions.

briefs.headline: Trump signs order to ease diesel costs, ‘save millions of dollars’ for farmers
briefs.deck: In response to rising diesel prices, US President Donald Trump has enacted an executive order designed to alleviate financial pressures across multiple sectors. This order is anticipated to substantially cut fuel costs for farmers and truck drivers, ultimately contributing to lower grocery prices. Additionally, it urges states to expand access to tax-free red-dyed diesel and consider lifting…
briefs.bodyText:
US President 
Donald Trump
 on Monday (local time) signed an executive order aimed to ease the burden of high diesel prices on farmers, truckers and other businesses, as fuel costs continue to put pressure on Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections.
Trump announced the move during a campaign stop in Grand Island, Nebraska, saying that loosening limits on the tax-free use of red-dyed diesel would save farmers “millions” and help bring down the cost of goods and groceries.
“Pete and Jim, this should absolutely ensure your election, I guarantee you that,” Trump said, addressing Republican governor Pete Ricketts and governor Jim Pillen.
The order directs states to increase the availability of tax-exempt red-dyed diesel, which is used in farming, construction and other industries. It also calls on states to consider waiving certain fuel taxes and includes so-called non-enforcement of dyed diesel limitations.
Red-dyed diesel is exempt from federal and state excise taxes. The administration says that temporarily easing restrictions would reduce costs for businesses that depend on diesel.
“The typical trucker will save more than $100 every time they fill up,” Trump said as he signed the order before a crowd in Grand Island.
“Farmers will also save millions and millions of dollars, and this order will also drive down the cost of all goods and to go to grocery prices very substantially.”
The steps also include the treasury department reviewing certain taxes on diesel.
Ten states accounting for roughly a third of US diesel sales had already taken steps to allow wider use of dyed diesel by Friday, according to research firm ClearView Energy Partners, cited by Politico. Several states had also waived taxes on diesel used in agricultural vehicles.
Diesel still costs well above last year
The move comes as diesel prices remain sharply higher than a year ago.
The average price of diesel fell to $6.32 a gallon on Monday, down 13 cents from the previous week but still $2.63 higher than a year ago, according to AAA.
Fuel prices have surged amid the ongoing war against Iran and Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. The conflicts have contributed to a significant decline in the amount of diesel available on the global market.
Exports of American diesel have also risen to record levels since the US and Israel launched a war with Iran in February and Ukraine began targeting Russian refineries.
Trump drops diesel export ban
The red-dyed diesel measure follows weeks of uncertainty over how the administration would respond to rising fuel prices.
Trump had repeatedly backed an outright ban on diesel exports as agriculture-state Republicans, including Iowa Senator Chuck Grassley, pushed for action to lower costs for farmers.
Energy secretary Chris Wright and White House energy advisers had been working on alternatives.
But on Friday, Trump ruled out a diesel export ban and said he had never really considered one, after Europe agreed to release fuel from its diesel reserves.
Agriculture secretary Brooke Rollins said Monday morning that Trump would announce additional short-term relief for farmers in Nebraska and that she would also discuss the issue during a stop in Iowa.
High fuel and grocery prices have become a major concern for rural voters, many of whom have backed Trump and Republicans in recent elections. Nebraska farmers and ranchers have also been angered by the administration's plan to allow more imports of foreign beef.
