briefs.headline: RBI swap scheme boosts private banks' Q2 business numbers
briefs.deck: Private banks witnessed considerable credit and deposit growth in the second quarter of FY27. This growth was driven by the RBI's concessional dollar-rupee swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits. Major banks like Axis Bank, Kotak, and HDFC Bank reported varying growth figures, showing the impact of international branches. Although headline numbers appeared strong, underlying growth was more moderate…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Private banks' Q2 FY27 credit and deposit growth got a significant lift from RBI's concessional dollar-rupee swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits. Banks mobilised billions of dollars and deployed part of the funds through overseas branches, boosting headline balance-sheet growth.
The gap between headline and underlying growth was significant. Axis Bank's advances grew 22.7%, but 18.8% excluding Rs 43,800 crore of FCNR-linked overseas loans; deposit growth fell to 17% from 20.7%. Kotak's advances grew 24.7% and deposits 23.2%, but underlying deposit growth was around 12.7% after excluding Rs 55,344 crore of FCNR(B) deposits, against which its overseas branches lent Rs 16,110 crore.
IDFC First Bank's gross advances grew 29.9%, against 20.4% domestically after excluding Rs 24,885 crore of IBU leverage. Deposit growth similarly fell to 17% from 25.9%. Yes Bank's credit growth moderated to 17.7% from 23.8% and deposit growth to 13.2% from 19.5% after adjusting for FCNR-linked lending/mobilisation.
HDFC Bank mobilised the most among the disclosed balances at $11.5 billion, with $5.7 billion of overseas loans and $3.1 billion of standby letters of credit against the deposits. Its advances grew 16.3% and deposits 18.8%. The June facility made FCNR mobilisation more attractive by allowing banks to swap the dollars with RBI at concessional rates. It boosted deposits directly and, through overseas lending, advances. The result was stronger headline growth, while normalised numbers show a more moderate but still healthy domestic trajectory.

briefs.headline: Govt likely to sign BIT with Saudi Arabia
briefs.deck: India plans to sign a bilateral investment treaty with Saudi Arabia, allowing quicker arbitration for investors. The exhaustion of legal remedies period has been reduced from five years to two years for Saudi Arabia. This decision is significant due to the interest of Saudi Aramco in investing in Indian refineries. The government aims to increase foreign direct investment inflows by making…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Government is likely to sign a bilateral investment treaty (BIT) with Saudi Arabia, allowing companies from the Gulf state to initiate international arbitration two years after they exhaust legal remedies in India. This is a concession from the current five-year clause in the model BIT finalised by govt a year ago.
The Union cabinet had discussed the model BIT last week and officials said for Saudi a two-year window was being provided at a time when Saudi Aramco is looking to invest in two refineries in the country, along with BPCL and ONGC. Besides, other investment plans are also lined up. In the past, govt has made concessions for UAE and Israel.
The move comes at a time when the Union cabinet will consider a proposal to reduce the period for exhaustion of legal remedies from five years. While the original plan was to reduce the period to one year, the decision in case of Saudi Arabia may result in this being extended to two years, officials indicated.
"We have a new template which will be approved (by cabinet) shortly. But in the meanwhile, we have not halted the process. 
We are negotiating with countries with a lot more of those elements which are in the new template," finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman said on Monday.
She said negotiations are underway with several countries, including Canada and Russia, on bilateral investment protection agreements. "If things go well, by Dec we should be concluding agreements with at least three more countries," she said at the Munich Security Conference, adding that negotiations with Canada could be concluded by Dec or early next year if they progress as expected. The amendment comes at a time when India is seeking to step up FDI inflows.

briefs.headline: Proposed GST changes positive for business: Experts
briefs.deck: Proposed changes to the GST regime are expected to benefit businesses, improving cash flow and refunds. A refund on accumulated GST for input services and capital goods may help manufacturers significantly. The GST Council will discuss the rationalization of ITC, which has long been an issue for businesses. Decriminalization of certain GST provisions aims to create a more business-friendly…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Tax experts see the proposed changes to the GST regime - that will now be discussed on Thursday -- as positive for businesses, helping reduce the working capital requirement and eventually benefit buyers.
"It is expected that businesses may be entitled for refund of accumulated GST on input services and capital goods, which is currently restricted to raw material. It is also expected that 90% of the refund claimed will be granted on a provisional basis within seven days. These proposals alone can relax the working capital stress in the range of 2-4% for manufacturers, eventually helping businesses reduce the product prices and invest funds back into business," said Pratik Jain, partner at consulting firm Price Waterhouse & Co.
Refunds and limited use of accumulated input tax credit (ITC) have been two major concerns for businesses. For long-gestation projects, GST Council members will discuss a proposal where tax paid on services and plant and machinery can now be refunded, with refund on the latter spread over five years. The process is also being reworked for exporters. According to govt data, 38,700 taxpayers claimed refund on exports, and 13,100 have paid taxes on plant and machinery.
 Among businesses claiming refund on an inverted rate structure, 15,200 have paid such tax on plant and machinery and 17,300 have paid tax on input services.
"ITC rationalisation is the need of the hour as credits locked up either due to restrictions in usage or due to the sellers' defaults or due to delayed ITC refunds add significantly to the working capital costs and easing credits and related refunds would make businesses more competitive. Providing regular refunds to capital intensive projects, such as semiconductors and refineries where ITC remains locked up for several years, would effectively reduce their capex requirements and encourage more investors to come forward and invest in long-gestation period projects," said MS Mani, partner at Deloitte India.
"Allowing GST incurred on various employee related expenses, such as insurance and cafeteria, as credit to businesses is going to be a major policy shift. This could result in direct benefit to large sections of the workforce and reduce paperwork for businesses," added Jain.
Govt officials said that decriminalisation and allowing courts to decide where a person should be arrested will really liberate businesses, who are often threatened. "Businesses seek an environment free from needless policing and hence the proposed removal of the arrest provisions and the softening of the prosecution provisions would go a long way in improving business confidence," said Mani.
"Decriminalising GST is a welcome move that honours the 90% of honest, law-abiding traders driving our economy. Ease of business shouldn't be stifled by constant fear of prosecution but bad actors must still face strict penalties," said Bangalore-based trade activist Sajjan Raj Mehta.

briefs.headline: Sir Dorabji Tata Trust asked to respond to Venu complaint in a week
briefs.deck: Maharashtra Charity Commissioner has requested Sir Dorabji Tata Trust to provide a response by October 12. Complaints were filed by vice-chairmen Venu Srinivasan and Vijay Singh regarding governance issues. They allege the trust has overstepped its charitable mandate by interfering in Tata Sons' affairs. The commissioner may decide to hold a hearing or rule based on submitted complaints. This…
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Maharashtra Charity Commissioner has asked the Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) to respond by Oct 12 to complaints from its vice-chairmen, Venu Srinivasan and 
Vijay Singh
, escalating an internal governance battle that could change how 
Tata Sons
 is controlled.
In separate complaints filed on Sept 25, Srinivasan and Singh alleged that SDTT had exceeded its charitable mandate by intervening in the commercial and strategic affairs of Tata Sons. SDTT is the largest shareholder in Tata Sons.
They had asked the commissioner to issue interim orders barring the trust from holding board meetings, restraining it from exercising its voting rights at Tata Sons' annual general meeting (AGM), suspending or removing trustees if violations are established, and stopping chairman Noel Tata from participating in Tata Sons board decisions in his capacity as a nominee director.
The commissioner can either hold a hearing involving both the complainants and respondents or decide the matter on the written complaints filed by Srinivasan and Singh and the written submissions made by SDTT, according to a person who is familiar with the proceedings.
The commissioner's decision to seek SDTT's response comes after chairman Noel Tata and his son, Neville Tata, an SDTT trustee, filed six caveats on Sept 30 to pre-empt adverse orders against the trust and themselves. 
The two, who are also trustees of six other Tata trusts that hold shares in Tata Sons, filed 30 more caveats. The 36 filings, running to 150 to 200 pages, invoked Sections 41D and 47 of the Maharashtra Public Trusts Act, which deal with the removal of trustees and suspension of a trust board, respectively, as well as Section 41E, which empowers authorities to restrain dealings involving trust property, in this case Tata Sons.
In May, the commissioner barred the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), the second-largest shareholder in Tata Sons, from holding board meetings after Srinivasan complained that its board composition violated the Act.
The complaint argued that three members of SRTT's then six-member board were perpetual trustees, above the statutory cap of 25% of a trust's board strength. The commissioner passed the order ex parte because SRTT had not filed a caveat and learned of the complaint only from the order.
Srinivasan and Singh's latest requests, if the commissioner entertains them, would upend the Tata Group's governance framework. Any interim order would curtail SDTT's functioning, impairing the two largest Tata Sons shareholders' ability to influence key governance decisions at the holding company.

briefs.headline: Škoda Auto India eyes record sales, targets 8-10% growth on strong market momentum
briefs.deck: The company plans to launch its first electric vehicle in India next year.
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI
Škoda Auto India is targeting 8-10% growth in sales this year, which would take the automaker to its highest-ever sales volume, despite facing a high base following last year’s GST-led demand surge, a senior company official said.
“Year till date, we are on a growth path of around 8%, which I think is quite good for us. With the facelift Slavia, I am expecting to end this year with an 8-10% growth,” said Ashish Gupta, Brand Director, Škoda Auto India.
The company had ended last year on a strong note following the reduction in GST rates, making the current year’s growth comparison challenging. Mr. Gupta said the market had been declining before the GST reforms, particularly in the smaller-car segment, but demand picked up sharply after the tax changes.
“Till August, the market has grown almost 23%, which is phenomenal,” Mr. Gupta said, adding that despite the high base from September-December last year, he expects the passenger vehicle market to register around 15% growth this year.
He also expects India’s passenger car market to cross 5 million units this year, significantly ahead of earlier industry expectations that the milestone would be reached only around 2029.
“All of us, with all our intelligence, were actually predicting that the market will hit 5 million by 2029, so it’s in a fast-forward mode now,” Mr. Gupta said. However, he cautioned that geopolitical and environmental uncertainties could affect the continuation of the current momentum.
For Škoda, the Slavia facelift is expected to provide an additional boost during the crucial festive season. The company had committed to introducing 10 product interventions during the year and has completed the programme with the launch of the updated sedan.
“The Slavia facelift has got very good reception. We introduced the car last month. We are launching it right at the start of the festive season, so that it will help us to push the volumes of the Slavia,” he said.
Škoda is also preparing for a significant shift in its product strategy. The company plans to launch its first electric vehicle in India next year, marking its entry into the country’s rapidly expanding EV market.

briefs.headline: flyadeal plans major India expansion, eyes Lucknow, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata

briefs.bodyText:
Saudi Arabia’s low-cost carrier flyadeal, part of Saudia Group, is planning a major expansion of its India network as air travel and tourism flows between India and Saudi Arabia continue to grow.

flyadeal is also evaluating flights connecting Saudi Arabia with Lucknow, Calicut, Delhi, Chennai and Kolkata, Sanjiv Kapoor, acting Chief Executive Officer of flyadeal and Executive Vice-President, Strategy at Saudia Group, said.

“We see tremendous potential to connect more travellers through convenient, affordable and reliable services,” Mr. Kapoor said.

As a member of the Saudia Group, the carrier is expected to play a growing role in supporting the Kingdom’s ambitions to attract more international visitors and expand its aviation and tourism sectors.

stories.headline: Sooryavanshi or Samson? India face selection dilemma
stories.deck: In one corner stands teen prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, whose fearless strokeplay has set pulses racing across the circuit. In the other is Sanju Samson, the seasoned campaigner whose heroics in India’s 2026 T20 World Cup triumph remains etched in cricketing folklore.
stories.bodyText:
LUCKNOW: Coming off the golden glow of their Asian Games triumph in Japan, India step into Tuesday’s fivematch T20I series opener against the West Indies at the Ekana Stadium here carrying momentum, silverware and an intriguing selection headache at the top of the order.
While Abhishek Sharma’s explosive presence as a designated opener is virtually etched in ink, the suspense lies in who walks out alongside him. It is a clash of narratives: the breathtaking audacity of youth versus the hardened composure of experience.
In one corner stands teen prodigy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, whose fearless strokeplay has set pulses racing across the circuit. In the other is 
Sanju Samson
, the seasoned campaigner whose heroics in India’s 2026 T20 World Cup triumph remains etched in cricketing folklore.
Will head coach Gautam Gambhir lean into the romance of the next generation, or will he trust the calm authority of a proven match-winner?
Bowling coach Morne Morkel acknowledged the delicate juggling act ahead of the first T20I. “I’m pretty sure Gautam will look to rotate him (Sooryavanshi). That is up to the selectors, and the coach and the captain, in terms of the playing level, or which playing level will be the best to win a game for India on our home soil. 
In terms of the starting X, he guys just came back from an Asian Games, so we’re going to see how everybody’s feeling after jet lag, after travelling, and then from there, make plans accordingly.”
Fatigue, indeed, remains a tangible hurdle. “The red flag, or the problem, might be our guys travelling back and then immediately playing an international match after the Asian Games,” Morkel said. “Some of the guys arrived only a couple of days ago. But I think once we are up and running, and the series gets going, we will be up for it.”
The spotlight will also be on skipper 
Shreyas Iyer
. In his last 10 outings at the helm, a half-century has eluded him. Iyer’s blade yielded just 34 runs across two Asian Games fixtures and 48 in three matches against Afghanistan.
Fortunately for India, their bowling arsenal welcomes back two electrifying local favourites returning to action after the Zimbabwe tour in July: Mayank Yadav and Prince Yadav.
Standing in India’s way is a dangerous West Indies outfit marshalled by Shai Hope, who is in blistering touch following back-to-back ODI centuries.
For the Caribbean side, Lucknow is a familiar venue. They spent nearly a month in the city in 2019 when Afghanistan used the Ekana Stadium as their home ground. stories.headline: Other side of Asian Games success: 201 athletes won just 6 bronze, 137 returned empty-handed
stories.deck: India's performance at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games included a total of 85 medals and a fourth-place finish. Despite this achievement, a significant number of athletes returned empty-handed, highlighting areas for improvement. A total of 137 athletes across 16 disciplines failed to secure any medals. Additionally, 201 athletes managed only six bronze medals across 22 disciplines, indicating low…
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India’s 85-medal haul at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games was its secondbest finish, but the headline numbers don’t reveal everything.
A sport-by-sport audit by TOI shows that 137 Indian athletes across 16 disciplines returned empty-handed, exposing persistent gaps in the country’s medal ambitions.
India’s pruned-down 495-member contingent competed across 36 sport disciplines and finished fourth with 21 gold, 27 silver and 37 bronze medals.
Yet 137 athletes across 16 disciplines won nothing.
Another 64 athletes across six sports managed six bronze — one each in kurash, mixed martial arts, rowing, sepaktakraw, soft tennis and wushu. The zero-medal list included canoeing (19 athletes), cycling (14), equestrian (7), esports (15), fencing (20), gymnastics (1), judo (3), karate (2), rugby sevens (13), sport climbing (2), surfing (4), swimming (12), taekwondo (3), tennis (7), teqball (3) and volleyball (12). The six-bronze group comprised kurash (6 athletes), MMA (2), rowing (22), sepaktakraw (21), soft tennis (6) and wushu (7).
In all, 201 athletes accounted for just six bronze medals across the 22 disciplines mentioned above. In other prominent sports with sizable athlete numbers, table tennis sent 10 athletes and returned with one bronze and badminton’s 20-member contingent managed one bronze in the men’s team event. 
Together, the two sent 37 athletes and produced only two bronze.
India contested in 259 medal events in AichiNagoya and won medals in just 20, a 7.7% eventpodium conversion rate. Of 356 medals available in which India featured, the nation collected 85, a conversion rate of only 23.9%.
The spending breakdown
The govt spent Rs 259.69 crore on 19 sports as part of the overall total expenditure during the current 
Asian Games
 cycle (Nov 2023-Aug 2026), led by badminton (Rs 49.26 cr), cycling track (Rs 35.9 cr), fencing (Rs 28.2 cr), table tennis (Rs 25.3 cr), tennis (Rs 22.4 cr) and canoe/kayak (Rs 20.1 cr). Other allocations included rowing (Rs 13.8 cr,) swimming (Rs 10.8 cr), gymnastics (Rs 10.49 cr), judo (Rs 8.05 cr), wushu (Rs 7.8 cr), volleyball (Rs 6.5 cr), sepaktakraw (Rs 5.7 cr), equestrian (Rs 3.7 cr), rugby (Rs 3.63 cr), surfing (Rs 2.9 cr), karate (Rs 1.99 cr), soft tennis (Rs 1.6 cr) and kurash (Rs 1.6 cr).
On three sports – MMA, eSports and sport climbing, the govt spent no money. As per the govt’s own estimates, it spent approximately Rs 703 cr across 30 disciplines during the Nov 2023-Aug 2026 preparation cycle. The Rs 703 cr included about Rs 118 cr for domestic training and national coaching camps, Rs 40 cr for overseas training, Rs 252 cr for international competition exposure, Rs 89 cr for equipment, Rs 86 cr for foreign coaches/support staff and Rs 118 cr for other expenses, including Indian experts, championships, competitions in India, grassroots and coach development.
Also, a total of 427 athletes who were part of the govt’s various programmes and schemes participated in the Games, including 77 athletes from Target Olympic Podium Scheme (TOPS) Core group, 78 from TOPS Development 78, 48 from Target Asian Games Group (TAGG), 65 Khelo India Athlete (KIA), 25 from National Centre of Excellence (NCoE) and 134 from National Coaching Camps (NCCs).
The Glasgow comparison is revealing, though not like-for-like. India had 122 athletes and para-athletes in 10 sports at the curtailed 2026 Commonwealth Games and won 39 medals — 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze — also finishing fourth. The Asian Games contingent was 4.06 times larger, but its 85-medal haul was only 2.18 times Glasgow’s. Medal efficiency was 17.2 per 100 athletes in Aichi-Nagoya against 32 in Glasgow.
The message is that at this level, the medal base remains concentrated.
For a country investing Rs 703 cr across a multi-year cycle, the next challenge is clear: turn wider participation, exposure and support into wider podium conversion.

stories.headline: Grit, gold and a house that kabaddi built
stories.deck: A player-turned-coach, Neeta Dadwe has spent decades learning the game, building teams and pushing the women’s game towards a promising future
stories.bodyText:
Gold. Silver. Bronze. Brass. It all gleams at you the moment you step inside. A towering cabinet blazes with medals, cups, and memorabilia, every piece neatly in its place. Flanking it stand trophies as tall as a small child, too big to fit anywhere and too important to hide. “Kabaddi gave me this house. Everything you see here is what the sport has given me. All of it is a result of my hard work,” declares Neeta Dadwe, pride lighting up her face.
To understand the woman behind that wall of silverware, step out of the house and onto the road that leads to it. A quiet bylane in the heart of the city, far from the roar of Hyderabad’s traffic, it tips steeply downhill, as if to remind you that you are indeed standing on the Deccan plateau.
At first glance, it’s unremarkable. Only, it isn’t. This is a roll call of Indian sport and power. Two-time Olympic medallist P.V. Sindhu, India’s first woman Grandmaster Koneru Humpy, and former cricketer Venkatapathy Raju all live in these bylanes. C.V. Anand, Telangana’s Director General of Police, is a resident too, while Karnam Malleswari, the first Indian woman to win an Olympic medal, once called it home.
And somewhere amid all that star power lives Neeta, who has just led India’s women’s kabaddi team to gold at the Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
The reinvention
An Arjuna Awardee with a stellar playing career, she reinvented herself as a coach and never looked back, guiding the national side to gold at the 2014 Asian Games and the 2016 South Asian Games.
Her name may not echo as loudly as those of her neighbours, but the shine of her achievements is every bit as bright. A day after she landed in the City of Pearls to a roaring welcome at the airport, The Hindu stepped into her cozy home for a conversation.
The Indian women’s kabaddi team defeated Iran 37-34 in a closely fought final, successfully defending the gold medal it won at the Hangzhou edition in 2022. As captain Pushpa Rana, all-rounder Jyoti Thakur and several other players revealed after the triumph in Japan, the groundwork for this success was laid at carefully planned training camps.
“Our first camp was at SAI Gandhinagar in May for one month. We had 42 girls and brought it down to 29 there, which was a tough task for us on the selection committee – which includes Mamata Poojary and V. Tejeswini Bai. The next camp was for 15 days, again at SAI Gandhinagar, while the third was at the JSW facility in Ballari,” Neeta recalled.
“We got stuff like a fitness trainer, masseur, sauna bath, ice bath, and more, which is not common for us in kabaddi. I was the coach in 2014 (Asian Games) and we didn’t have as many facilities as we got this time. The kids were very happy because our camps were like international ones. And because of that, for probably the first time, we barely had any injuries during the tournament.”
No mobiles, please
Besides physical and mental training, video analysis and tactical discussions, the team followed a ‘no mobile phones’ policy during the camps.
“We asked the federation and got their permission to do it. The more you use your mobile, especially later in the night, the more you will feel tired the next day. We got the players very much involved in it. One girl would take turns to collect the phones and deposit them. They would get them on Saturday and by Sunday’s end, they would be returned.”
What they could not prepare for, and what has since been widely reported, were the poor living conditions that awaited them. The entire contingent was put up on a docked cruise ship, and it wasn’t as luxurious as it sounds.
“The schedule was very tight for us, and the ground was very far from the ship where we were put up. To be honest, not everyone fits [in the accommodation provided] on the ship. Food was also an issue. Non-vegetarians didn’t have a problem, but the vegetarians faced many. However, the girls managed to face it all without many complaints,” Neeta explained, adding that bread became a staple of her diet there.
On the mat, however, things were largely smooth. The side breezed past its group-stage and semifinal opponents before running into a familiar rival, Iran, in the final. India made a bright start and raced to a 5-2 lead, before Iran levelled with a super tackle and surged ahead 7-5.
In the side’s closest contest in Japan, it had a vocal crowd behind it, including members of the Indian Olympic Association, headlined by its president P.T. Usha.
“P.T. Usha came to watch our match. The whole of IOA came. We were all very tense. I was so tense that I couldn’t even look back [at the stands]. The girls and I were under a lot of pressure, but we all had the same goal, which was to win the gold medal,” she admitted.
“In 2018 we won silver. Besides that, we won gold in 2010, 2014, and 2022. I was very scared and worried about how we would fare this time. Not just because of past results, but also because we selected a strong team this time and had good camps.”
Among the things that helped the team get past the Iranians was video footage of their time in India in the months leading up to the Asiad.
“They had been practicing in India for two months. They were in Himachal, played with two or three clubs in Haryana. We asked the federation for some of their videos, and we studied them well.”
For this Asian Games, Neeta was assisted by Mamata, someone she had coached extensively before, including at the 2014 edition of the continental competition. While that familiarity helped in discussing tactics, the two also shared the same nervous tension as the campaign kicked off.
“We used to sit at night and map on a piece of paper who should be played where. And on the first day there, neither of us slept because we were tense. If we used Ritu Negi in the corner pool, then they [the opponents] would’ve made a strategy for it. So we changed things up to give others some food for thought. In the end, we were working towards bringing the country a medal. We were not playing for our States or for Railways or anything. We were representing India.”
Neeta has coached the Indian women’s side to two Asian Games golds, but can’t bring herself to compare both. “Zameen aasman ka farak hai” (a world of difference) came the declaration.
“The emotions involved are very different. In 2018, Iran edged India narrowly in the final. They were coached by our very own Shailaja Jain, who taught them exactly how to play against us. Also, there is a lot more competition now. Look at how well Nepal (lost to India in the semifinals) did. No one expected that.”
Having excelled as a player and a coach, how does Neeta compare the two experiences? “A player and a coach are different. A player gets to enjoy more; I was one, I know it very well,” she grinned.
Neeta the player greatly helped Neeta the coach. She channelled those experiences to help gel better with the team and structure training sessions in ways that kept players wholeheartedly involved. That also included keeping the workload relatively light in the days leading up to the tournament.
Fitness, however, was one area where there were no compromises.
“When I was a player, we used to make a fitness schedule. And on the days we had to do fast training or speed workouts, those days we used to cry or make excuses. So I told my girls upfront that I did not want to hear any excuses. I said we are all working towards a common goal and that they can express their feelings freely. And to be fair, they also supported me well in this endeavour.”
Professional pathway
While interest in kabaddi took off with the launch of the Pro Kabaddi League in 2014, it is the men who have reaped the rewards, while the women’s ecosystem is yet to get an equivalent. A Women’s Kabaddi Challenge was held in 2016, but it was a flash in the pan.
“In 2016, we had the Kabaddi Challenge, but it took place in the men’s court. If there are three steps in a women’s court, there are five in the men’s court. And many argued that since volleyball and basketball have same-sized courts for men and women, why not kabaddi? But I believe that if that Challenge took place in a women’s court, it would have been a big success,” she opined, adding, “If Pro Kabaddi starts for girls, it will be beneficial as more kids will come out in the ecosystem.”
PKL’s format has allowed the best international stars to ply their trade in India, which has not only helped coaches here understand how they operate but also helped Indian players improve by rubbing shoulders with them. Neeta believes the same knock-on effect would carry over to women.
“Besides getting to know the foreign players better, we will also get better in terms of fitness, nutrition, and more. Pro Kabaddi also provides players with great facilities; I have seen it. In India, after cricket, it is kabaddi only.”
That said, Neeta explained that the women have enough tournaments to keep them busy all year round.
“We had the World Cup earlier. From 21st to 31st this month, we have the Commonwealth Kabaddi Championship in Ahmedabad. After that, we have the Indo-Asian Games in Dubai in November. After that, there’s the World Cup again. There is something or the other continuously; it’s not like before.”
“Kabaddi, as you know, is not a game for rich people. I have seen kids come from nothing. Take Aslam (Inamdar) and so many other boys and girls. He told me that there was a time when he did not even get to eat; only he knows what all his mother did for him. He told me his story. If kids benefit from [getting a professional league], it’s a matter of pride for them. They can then come up in life thanks to kabaddi.”
The Indian women’s kabaddi team has clearly benefited from a coach who has walked many a mile in their shoes, back when chances were rare, the spotlight was dim, and the money was thin. That road made Neeta who she is.
And as the interview wound down, she threw in a reminder that it wasn’t time for her to rest just yet. For she had already packed for the next stretch: a family road trip to her hometown, Nagpur, home to a local club, the Maratha Lancers, which first lit the fuse on her career.
Back in Hyderabad, the cabinet will keep blazing, and the trophies too big to fit anywhere will stand guard. Neeta, meanwhile, took to the highway, carrying her gold home to where it all began. Because for a champion, no stage shines quite like the place that made her.

stories.headline: Messi set for emotional Argentina farewell in Buenos Aires friendly vs Benin
stories.deck: The 39-year-old superstar will play his final match for Argentina on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) — a friendly against Benin at Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires — marking a pivotal moment in the country's football
stories.bodyText:
Argentina fans are confident there is a bright future beyond Lionel Messi as the team's most influential player of the last two decades prepares to bid farewell.
The 39-year-old superstar will play his final match for Argentina on Tuesday (October 6, 2026) — a friendly against Benin at Estadio Monumental in Buenos Aires — marking a pivotal moment in the country's football.
Messi leaves behind an extraordinary legacy, including the 2022 World Cup title, two more World Cup finals (2014, 2026), two Copa América trophies (2021, 2024), an Olympic gold medal (2008), and 125 goals as the national team's all-time leading scorer.
His international retirement raises an inevitable question: Can Argentina remain among the global elite, or is a long trophy drought — reminiscent of the 35-year dry spell following Diego Maradona's departure — on the horizon?
“Messi leaves behind something unequaled,” national coach Lionel Scaloni says. “We have to keep playing, but the feeling of having him on the pitch is unique. I've never seen anyone else convey what he does on a football field, and that is what we're going to miss.”
However, Scaloni — who is in advanced negotiations to renew his contract for another four years — looks beyond Messi with optimism: “The Argentine national team will endure. We will remain at a high level, I have no doubt about that.”
The future is hereIn the first two post-World Cup matches without Messi, Argentina dazzled in the past week with resounding victories against Bolivia 4-0 and Burkina Faso 7-0. Despite the opponents' stature, the matches offered compelling glimpses of what lies ahead.
Alongside established stars like Emiliano Martínez, Cristian Romero, Enzo Fernández, and Lautaro Martínez, an exciting wave of new talent emerged — creative midfielders Nicolás Paz and Franco Mastantuono, and wingers Gianluca Prestianni and Leonel Flores.
Flores is a Boca Juniors youth player who made his professional debut just two months ago and has already earned senior national team experience.
“There's a changing of the guard; maybe we have to play differently now, not thinking in terms of Messi and 10 others,' but rather as a unified team,” supporter Cristian Versalles, 55, told the AP after watching the victory over Burkina Faso on Saturday.
His son, Ramiro, 23, added, “Given the number of players coming through, there's definitely a new generation ready to step up. Nico Paz is the heir apparent." Paz, playing out of Italian club Como, was one of the scorers.
Also at the friendly and wearing the No. 19 jersey — the same one Messi wore during his senior national team debut in 2005 — 10-year-old fan Uzzi Rivero admitted, “It makes me really sad that he doesn't play for Argentina anymore.” However, the youngster scowled at the suggestion that Argentina might face a trophy-less era following Messi's retirement.
Another fan, Valentina Gago, 20, said: “I'm excited about Argentina without Messi; my favorite player is Lautaro Martínez. It's not the same as Messi but I love him just the same.”
With his goal against Burkina Faso, Inter Milan captain Lautaro Martínez ranks as Argentina's third-highest all-time goal-scorer with 42.
“As long as the players are eager to give their all for the shirt, for me, Argentina will remain a contender,” Gago said.
The world will find out at the 2028 Copa América.

briefs.headline: 'No one treats a human being like that': Shastri on Pakistan's Imran Khan treatment
briefs.deck: Former Indian captain and head coach Ravi Shastri has criticised the reported treatment of jailed former Pakistan captain Imran Khan, calling it “inhumane” amid concerns over his health and vision. Shastri said Khan deserves better treatment, praised his leadership and 1992 World Cup triumph, and described him as one of Pakistan’s most recognised global figures.
briefs.bodyText:
Former India head coach 
Ravi Shastri
 has spoken out over the reported treatment of jailed former Pakistan captain 
Imran Khan
, calling it “inhumane” and saying no person should be treated that way.
Reports cited in the story claim Khan’s health has worsened in jail, with only 15% vision remaining in his right eye.
Shastri backs Imran on humanitarian grounds
Speaking to Republic World, Shastri said he was shocked by Khan’s situation and believed cricketers around the world would share his concerns.
"I'm not a politician. But just to see the way he's being treated today is shocking. You know, no one treats a human being like that. On humanitarian grounds, I don't think he deserves what he's getting. So I don't speak just for myself. I think there'll be a lot of cricketers around the globe who will be echoing the same sentiments," said Shastri.
He also wished Khan good health and praised his achievements as a cricketer and captain, particularly his ability to guide young players.
"I just hope he's well and his health is good. Because what he gave to the game was something special. And my memories of him are just being an outstanding leader. You know, just a leader of men. The ability to motivate youngsters and then take them through. You said he came close at the age of 40, captain of the side, and he won the World Cup with a pretty young team," he added.
'He doesn't deserve it'
Shastri said Khan, who has been in jail since 2023, is one of Pakistan’s most recognisable figures worldwide and should receive better treatment.
"Hopefully. Hope he comes out and is treated better. He's been there for a long time. You could be out somewhere else, in the same position, because I don't understand the politics. But to sit in a cell there, he doesn't deserve it because he's the most recognised Pakistani face globally. 
Whether you like it or not, that's my view," said Shastri.
He also remembered Khan as a great all-rounder and leader, saying the India-Pakistan rivalry was built on mutual respect.
"This man you're seeing there with me was an unbelievable cricketer. I mean, a great cricketer is an understatement. The rivalry was out of respect."

briefs.headline: 'Fear may never completely go away': Kalkal on turning Olympic heartbreak into Asiad gold
briefs.deck: Sujeet Kalkal's Asian Games gold came two years after floods in Dubai cost him a chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics. The 25-year-old wrestler fought back from 2-9 down to beat Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev 10-9 in the 65kg final, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games. Now targeting Los Angeles 2028, Kalkal says he does not want to go to the Olympics just to…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Two years ago, Sujeet Kalkal was stranded at Dubai International Airport, watching his Olympic dream slip away with every passing hour.
On his way to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, for the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament, Kalkal was stuck in Dubai for three days after floods disrupted his travel plans. By the time a flight was arranged, it was too late. He could not reach Bishkek in time, and with it went his chance to qualify for the Paris Olympics.
Two years later, the disappointment of Dubai has been replaced by an 
Asian Games
 gold. Kalkal, the world No. 2 in the men's 65kg category, fought back from 2-9 down against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev in the final to win 10-9, ending India's eight-year wait for a wrestling gold at the Games.
The comeback was symbolic of what Kalkal's career has looked like since that Olympic setback. He has had to rebuild, compete through the disappointment and find a way back to the biggest stages. On Sunday, he did that with an Asian Games title.
When the final whistle came, Kalkal folded his hands, looked up and thanked God. He then took a lap of the arena with the Indian tricolour draped around his shoulders, tears and a broad smile.
For a wrestler who had once been denied even the chance to fight for an Olympic place, the moment carried a little more weight than an Asian Games gold.
"This gold means a lot to me. Not just because it is an Asian Games gold, but because there is so much behind this medal. The last few years have had many ups and downs, and I missed a few opportunities, but I never lost belief in myself," Kalkal told TimesofIndia.com in an exclusive interview on his way back to Imlota village in Bhiwani, Haryana, where his parents were waiting to welcome him.
Sujeet Kalkal (Image credit: PTI) 
The Dubai episode, he says, is now behind him. What remains is the lesson from it - and a much bigger target.
"Paris was very difficult for me to miss, but that experience made me stronger instead of breaking me. LA 2028 is obviously a very big goal for me," Kalkal said.
And he is clear about what he wants from that opportunity. "Olympics mein jaana hai toh sirf participate karne ke liye nahi jaana, bhaisaab. Gold ke liye jaana hai [“If you’re going to the Olympics, don’t go just to participate, brother. Go there to win gold]."
India had not won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games since 2018. Kalkal's victory ended that wait and added another major title to a career that already includes an U23 World Championship crown, Asian Championships success and a Zagreb Open triumph.
"India has won a wrestling gold at the Asian Games after eight years, so being a part of it is very special for me. This medal reminds me that if you keep working hard, your time will come," he said.
The road to the Asian Games gold was not easy for Kalkal. He had a challenging draw, but handled each bout with confidence.
After a comfortable opening victory, he made a statement in the quarterfinals by throwing Iran's Abbas Ebrahimzadehsavadkouhi from a standing position within the opening 20 seconds.
The semifinal brought an even bigger test, but Kalkal overcame Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka to reach the gold medal bout.
Then came the final against Tajikistan's Abdulmazhid Kudiev, and it looked like the toughest challenge of them all.
Instead of allowing the deficit to affect him, Kalkal fought his way back into the contest. He produced eight points to turn a seven-point deficit into a 10-9 victory and seal the Asian Games title.
"The simple plan was to wrestle my own way and not be impressed by my opponent's name. Whether he is an Olympic champion, a world champion or anyone else, everyone starts from zero on the mat. I just trusted my preparation and my strength. I knew that if I executed my best, I could beat anyone. Instead of thinking too much during the match, I just had to fight for every single point," he said.
Sujeet Kalkal during his gold medal bout (Image credit: PTI)
Kalkal also dedicated the gold to the country and remembered his father, who stood by him throughout his journey.
"I dedicate this gold to the whole of India. Of course, my first call was to my father. He has supported me tremendously throughout this journey, and without his support, it would have been impossible for me to reach this point. His support will always remain with me," the Indian wrestler said.
The final also reflected the mental change Kalkal says came from the disappointment of 2024.
"Fear may never completely go away, but now I know how to fight with fear. When you go through tough situations in life, small things stop bothering you. What happened in Dubai, missing the Olympic qualifiers - every experience taught me something," the Indian wrestler said.
"Now I don't run away from pressure. I enjoy pressure because those are the moments when you realise how strong you actually are," Kalkal said.
The Asian Games gold now joins an already impressive list of achievements for Kalkal, but he is not dwelling on the medals he has already won. The next target is Los Angeles. And this time, he wants to get there on his own terms.
"Gold ke liye jaana hai."

briefs.headline: Head coach Zidane celebrates first home win as France crush Belgium at Nations League
briefs.deck: France staged a stunning late comeback to beat Belgium 4-1 in the Nations League, giving Zinedine Zidane his first home win as coach. Belgium led until the 77th minute, but substitutes Désiré Doué, Rayan Cherki and Michael Olise scored four times. Italy beat Turkey 3-1, while Sweden defeated Romania 1-0 with Victor Gyökeres scoring again.
briefs.bodyText:
France scored four times in the final 14 minutes to beat Belgium 4-1 in the Nations League on Monday, giving 
Zinedine Zidane
 his first home victory as national coach.
Belgium looked on course for a surprise win after Dodi Lukébakio put them ahead in the 35th minute. But France’s substitutes changed the game late on, with Désiré Doué, Rayan Cherki and Michael Olise scoring four goals between the 77th and 91st minutes.
France turn game around late
Doué levelled with a low shot in the 77th minute before Cherki’s effort took a strange deflection off Belgium goalkeeper Maarten Vandevoordt to put France ahead.
Olise then scored twice in three minutes to complete a remarkable comeback.
“Tonight, this is soccer, this is what we love,” Zidane said. “We faced some difficulties in the first half but that’s part of the game; it’s the kind of match you get from time to time. It’s good to set things right — which is what we did — and we managed to play an extraordinary second half.”
Zidane praised his substitutes and the overall team effort.
“We knew the substitutes could change the game because they are high-quality players,” Zidane said. “But, once again, it was a complete team performance; while the substitutes might have made the difference when they came on, everyone has been good over these past two weeks — everyone played their part, and that’s what stands out to me.”
The result kept France top of Group A1, three points ahead of Italy, who beat Turkey 3-1. Belgium are third, four points behind France.
“It’s a collective effort, too,” Olise said. "He (Zidane) brings in ideas, we follow them — we’ve done that well over the last four matches, we’re going to continue like this."
Italy and Sweden also win
Italy recovered from Turkey’s equaliser to win 3-1, with Gianluca Scamacca, Riccardo Calafiori and Pio Esposito scoring.
Meanwhile, Victor Gyökeres scored again as Sweden beat Romania 1-0. It was his seventh straight Nations League match with a goal and his fourth of the campaign.
Northern Ireland stayed top of Group B2 after a 0-0 draw with Georgia, while Hungary beat Ukraine 2-1.

briefs.headline: 'We all have huge sympathy': Why England cricket ready to fund West Indies Test
briefs.deck: The ECB could provide financial support to Cricket West Indies to ensure England’s women play a Test in the Caribbean next spring. The match is viewed as vital preparation for the 2027 Ashes, with England seeking more red-ball cricket. Despite CWI’s financial difficulties and recent cost-cutting measures, the Test and wider multi-format tour remain on schedule.
briefs.bodyText:
The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) could step in financially if needed to ensure England’s women play a Test in the West Indies next spring. The match is planned as part of a multi-format series and is considered important preparation for England’s 2027 Ashes campaign.
Cricket West Indies (CWI) recently announced several cost-cutting measures, including reductions in player contracts. Earlier this year, it also cancelled a planned women’s Test against Australia, although the rest of that tour went ahead.
There have been no talks about cancelling England’s Test, and the wider tour, which includes three T20s and three ODIs, is not currently under threat.
Speaking to the BBC, ECB chair Richard Thompson said: "I hope not. That's not expected to be cancelled. I hope it will take place."
He also said the ECB would "look at" providing financial help if CWI faced difficulties staging the match.
Normally, the host cricket board pays the costs of hosting visiting teams. However, touring in the Caribbean can be expensive because players often need to travel between different islands. CWI said it has spent more than $80m on domestic air travel over the past 15 years.
'It's very important for us'
Thompson said the ECB wants the Test to happen because England need more red-ball cricket before the Ashes.
"We want that Test match to play out," said Thompson. "It's very important for us because our first women's match in the Ashes is the Headingley Test, so we need a good red-ball warm-up.
"We've got to be playing somewhere and we'd much prefer that to be the West Indies."
England have played just one Test since their Ashes defeat in early 2025, losing to India at Lord’s. They have not faced West Indies in a women’s Test since 1979, while West Indies last played a Test in 2004.
England will also hold a 10-day red-ball training camp in India in January as part of their Ashes preparations.
Thompson added: "We all have a huge sympathy for the West Indies, we all want to see a successful West Indian nation. They have very unique challenges and I hope through the International Cricket Council and others we can find a way through this."

briefs.headline: Ronaldo moved on from Portugal? Al-Nassr return comes with telling smile
briefs.deck: Cristiano Ronaldo has returned to Al-Nassr training after leaving Portugal’s camp amid his dispute with Jorge Jesus. The 41-year-old was pictured smiling with teammates as the Saudi club prepares to face Al-Diriyah. Jesus has left the door open for Ronaldo’s international return, but the final decision rests with the forward, who says he will explain his departure 'in due time'.
briefs.bodyText:
Cristiano Ronaldo
 returned to Al-Nassr training with a broad smile, offering his clearest indication yet that his attention has already shifted away from the controversy surrounding Portugal. Just one day after Portugal secured another Nations League victory without him, the 41-year-old forward was back at his club and preparing for the next challenge, leaving the growing discussion over Jorge Jesus behind him for now.
Ronaldo returns to Al-Nassr after leaving Portugal camp
Ronaldo rejoined his Al-Nassr teammates on Monday after leaving the Portugal camp during the international window, arriving back in Riyadh the previous Sunday with his family.
The Portuguese forward reported to the club's training centre four days before Al-Nassr's Saudi Roshn League meeting with Al-Diriyah, with the club publishing photographs of Ronaldo smiling and taking part in training. Ronaldo himself also shared images from the session
The images showed the 41-year-old back among his teammates and involved in the session, giving Al-Nassr supporters a first look at their captain following the disruption surrounding his Portugal departure.
The forward played only 67 minutes during Portugal's 1-0 win against Wales, meaning Al-Nassr will hope to have their captain available when the domestic campaign resumes.
Ronaldo's return comes after an increasingly public dispute with Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus, which began when the forward remained an unused substitute during the team's 2–1 victory over Norway despite warming up for around 30 minutes.
Ronaldo subsequently left the national team camp and returned to his club, leaving questions over whether the episode could affect his international future.
With Al-Nassr now preparing to face Al-Diriyah in the eighth round of the Saudi Pro League, Ronaldo's immediate attention has returned to club football and continuing the team's positive run.
Jorge Jesus leaves Portugal return entirely in Ronaldo's hands
While Ronaldo was returning to Al-Nassr, Jesus was addressing the situation publicly after Portugal's latest victory over Norway.
The Portugal coach refused to apologise for his decision to leave Ronaldo on the bench and made clear that he remains responsible for deciding which players start and which players enter the match.
Jesus nevertheless left the door open for Ronaldo to return during the next international window, provided the veteran forward remains active and performs for Al-Nassr.
“For me, Cris, in the next call-up, if he's playing at Al-Nassr, he'll be a player who can be called up.”
He later made it clear that the ball is firmly in Ronaldo’s court, with the decision on whether he returns ultimately his to make. Jesus said: “If he wants to, he'll return to the national team. We can talk before the next call-up, but Cris is the one who's going to decide.
The situation has consequently left Ronaldo with the final say over whether his Portugal career continues, while the reasons behind his departure from the camp remain unclear. When announcing his decision to leave, Ronaldo said he would explain the reasons that motivated him 'in due time', leaving the full story still to be told.
Ronaldo and Jesus have already shared success at Al-Nassr
The latest dispute is particularly notable because Ronaldo and Jesus already have a successful history together at Al-Nassr.
The pair worked together during the 2025–26 season and helped the Saudi club win the Saudi Pro League title, giving Ronaldo another major achievement during his time in Saudi Arabia.
Portugal have also moved forward successfully through the group stage, with Ronaldo featuring for 67 minutes in the win over Wales before being substituted. Jesus' team then beat Norway and Denmark before defeating Norway again 2–1 on Sunday
The result gave Portugal four wins from four matches in the 2026–27 UEFA Nations League and made them the first team to officially secure qualification for the quarter-finals.
Portugal now sit at the top of League A Group 4 with 12 points from a possible 12, maintaining a perfect record under their new coaching set-up.
Ronaldo, meanwhile, has returned to a club preparing for the next domestic test, with Al-Nassr scheduled to face Bruno Lage's Al-Diriyah on Friday evening.
For now, the picture is remarkably simple, because Ronaldo is back with Al-Nassr, Jesus has left the international decision with him, and the forward has given no public indication that he has decided to end his Portugal career.

briefs.headline: Good, not good enough: On India and the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026
briefs.deck: Without raising sports standards, India should not bid for hosting Olympics
briefs.bodyText:
Aspiring to host the Olympic Games in 2036, India faced a harsh reality check at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Compared with the previous Hangzhou Games, where it won 106 medals with a 650-plus contingent, the country won 85 medals from around 500 athletes. The aggregate fell short of an internally projected figure of around 100 medals. It is likely to invite a thorough postmortem, given the hundreds of crores of public money spent on the athletes’ preparation. India laboured to 21 gold medals, seven fewer than in Hangzhou, after a late surge of 11 top honours in the last two days, driven by the exploits of archers, boxers, wrestlers, and hockey and cricket players. It tied with Uzbekistan but managed to retain its fourth spot on the strength of a bigger haul of silver. Thirteen of the gold medals came from team events, with cricket, kabaddi and hockey making a clean sweep of titles. It underscored a stark reality: the country needs to raise its bar in medal-fetching individual sports, such as athletics, swimming, gymnastics, fencing and cycling, which determine success in multi-disciplinary Games. China, the runaway winner with a massive aggregate of 341 medals, including 169 gold, secured 54 medals in swimming alone. Barring athletics, India stood nowhere.
On a brighter note, India fielded 310 debutants and recorded a marginal increase in its athlete-to-medal ratio ahead of Los Angeles 2028. Several historic performances provided reasons to rejoice. Seventeen-year-old rookie recurve archer Kumkum Mohod dismantling the Korean women’s hegemony to help the archery team contribute five gold medals was a defining moment. Trap shooter Neeru Dhanda, golfer Pranavi Urs, wrestler Sujeet Kalkal and the women’s hockey team, which upset Paris Olympics silver medallist China to clinch gold after 44 years, hogged the limelight. Lovlina Borgohain, Aman Sehrawat, Mirabai Chanu, Vithya Ramraj and Gulveer Singh lived up to their billing. Boxers, wrestlers and golfers registered noticeable improvement. Olympic quota places in archery and hockey added to the excitement. Indian women catching up with men — both genders delivered 38 medals apiece — was another encouraging sign. On the flip side, India’s two major contributors, athletics and shooting, which earned 24 and 15 medals, respectively, yielded 12 fewer medals than in 2023. The shuttlers slipped, while the tennis players returned empty-handed after 40 years. P.V. Sindhu and Manu Bhaker flopped. Stricter scrutiny of athletes’ funding and efficient implementation of the revamped Khelo India scheme, designed with a long-term vision, are essential for course correction. Without propelling India’s sporting standards, a bid to host the Olympics may become a countdown to international embarrassment.

briefs.headline: India looks to bounce back as it faces Uruguay
briefs.deck: Nunez will pose the most obvious threat to the Blue Tigers’ defence; For Jamil, the challenge is to restore belief in the home side
briefs.bodyText:
The most high-profile international chapter in Indian football ends with perhaps its most intriguing test when the national team meets two-time World champion Uruguay at the Salt Lake Stadium on Tuesday. The Blue Tigers have already faced Panama and Brazil in this window, holding the Central Americans to a 1-1 draw before suffering a 0-4 defeat at the hands of the five-time World Cup winner. Uruguay provides another test of how far Khalid Jamil’s side can compete against an opponent with considerably greater stature and international experience.
Jamil has a squad built around experience and emerging players. Forward Ryan Williams, who gave up his Australian citizenship to play for India, will be the the principal attacker after scoring against Panama. Manvir Singh, Edmund Lalrindika and Vikram Partap Singh provide further options in the final third.
In midfield, Anirudh Thapa’s return adds experience alongside Apuia and Sahal Abdul Samad. After the lessons of the Brazil game, India will need discipline without the ball and greater efficiency when opportunities arrive. Anwar Ali, Abhishek Singh Tekcham, Bijoy Varghese and Akash Mishra form the backline, while goalkeeper Gurpreet Singh Sandhu needs to bounce back after a rather poor outing against Brazil.
Beginning a new chapter under former star Diego Forlan, Uruguay will look to build on its 4-1 victory over South Korea on September 28. Forlan is in his first international window as head coach and has already seen his team respond strongly on the Asian tour. After a 3-1 defeat by Japan, Uruguay outplayed South Korea, with Darwin Nunez scoring twice in Seoul.
Nunez will pose the most obvious threat to India’s defence, but Forlan will be without some of his biggest names. Federico Valverde and Giorgian de Arrascaeta are missing through injury.
For Jamil, the challenge is to restore belief in the Indian side by demonstrating that it can restrict a celebrated opponent and punish it when chances arise.
Uruguay last met India in Kolkata during the 1982 Nehru Gold Cup, winning 3-1 at the Eden Gardens. Forty four years later, La Celeste returns to the city, but the stakes are different. For India, it is another occasion to measure the distance between itself and one of world football’s established powers, and perhaps narrow it even if only for one evening.

briefs.headline: Mhatre appointed Mumbai vice-captain, cold shoulder for Suryakumar
briefs.bodyText:
Promising opener Ayush Mhatre has been handed a leadership role for the new Ranji Trophy season, being appointed vice-captain to the experienced Siddhesh Lad, while former captain Suryakumar Yadav has been left out of the squad for the season-opener against Chandigarh at the Wankhede Stadium from October 11.
Mhatre, who led India Under-19 to the World Cup title, has been earmarked for a larger role as Mumbai look to blend experience with youth. Chief selector Rajesh Pawar said the teenager’s form and cricketing acumen made him an obvious choice.
“The selection committee unanimously has gone with experienced Siddhesh Lad as the captain for the season. Along with a senior, we have planned to groom a junior in Ayush Mhatre as the vice-captain. He has led India U-19 to the World Cup win, is a smart cricketer and is in excellent nick,” Pawar said after an hour-long meeting, also attended by captain Lad, head coach Omkar Salvi and cricket advisor Dilip Vengsarkar.
Suryakumar, India’s T20 World Cup-winning captain, had made himself available for selection but has not been considered for the opening fixture as Mumbai prioritise giving their younger players an opportunity and want him to regain his red-ball rhythm first.
“Surya is available but it was thought to go with the youngsters for the time being. He is obviously a big-match player and a proven performer for Mumbai. We just want to get into rhythm by playing a few red-ball matches,” Pawar said.
“Suryakumar hasn’t played a red-ball match for the last 18 months, so we want him to have a few games under his belt and then he can get into the team.”
Mumbai will also have to do without Shardul Thakur, who led them last season. The lead pacer has suffered a slight fracture to his right middle finger during a training session and is expected to miss at least the first two matches.
Yashasvi Jaiswal, however, will feature in the opener, with Pawar welcoming the India batter’s availability. “It is very good that Yashasvi is playing the season-opener. He also needs game-time and the team will also benefit,” he said.
The squad: Siddhesh Lad (Capt.), Yashasvi Jaiswal, Ayush Mhatre (Vice-capt.), Divyaansh Saxena, Musheer Khan, Sarfaraz Khan, Suved Parkar, Aakash Anand (wk), Hardik Tamore (wk), Shams Mulani, Tanush Kotian, Atharva Ankolekar, Tushar Deshpande, Mohit Avasthi, Sylvester Dsouza, Onkar Tarmale.
